papers.title: Influence of natural and anthropogenic forcings on western US winter fire weather and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires
papers.authors: Srivastava, A., Risser, M., Ullrich, P., Wehner, M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Winter fire weather is shaped by interactions between anthropogenic climate change and natural climate variability, yet how the combination of human and natural forcings influences winter fire weather conditions remains poorly quantified. This study uses a multiple linear regression framework that removes long-term CO 2 -related trends to examine the influence of natural modes of variability on the December–February monthly fire weather index over the western United States (WUS), with the January 2025 Los Angeles (LA) fire risk as a motivating case study. Results show that the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Pacific North American pattern (PNA) and Atlantic Meridional Mode (AMM) significantly influence winter fire weather across the WUS, whereas the influence of CO 2 is more pronounced and generally significant over the interior regions, but less evident along the coastal areas of the WUS. Positive phases of the PNA and AMM, combined with La Niña–like conditions during December 2024 and January 2025, significantly elevated fire weather risk across southern California, including LA County. The elevated fire-weather conditions preceding the January 2025 fires in LA and surrounding regions were aggravated by the combined influence of the natural and anthropogenic modes. Our study also shows that anthropogenic CO 2 is associated with an estimated 10%–20% increase in the chances of the 2024–25 fire weather over the WUS coastal states, although this contribution is not statistically significant, while La Niña and positive PNA significantly increase these chances by at least 20% across California and by more than twice across much of the WUS, including southern California and neighboring states. We find that large-scale natural climate modes combined with increases in greenhouse gas concentration provide valuable information for understanding and predicting WUS winter fire weather.

papers.title: Movement characteristics of persistent extreme precipitation events over China during the warm season using high spatiotemporal resolution data
papers.authors: Liu, K., Mao, J., Wang, X., Ren, J.
papers.abstract: Abstract Moving persistent extreme precipitation events (PEPEs) can cause severe disasters along their tracks. However, a PEPE typically consists of multiple rain cells that evolve and move differently from one another, rendering the conventional single-center tracking method incapable of capturing their respective characteristics. Here we use a multi-rain cell tracking method to characterize the movement of PEPEs during the warm season (May to September) over China, utilizing high-resolution precipitation data at half‐hourly temporal and 0.1° spatial resolutions for the period 1998–2024. Based on the movement distance and direction, PEPEs are clustered into the long-distance eastward-moving, short-distance eastward-moving, northeastward-moving, and westward-moving types, which are most prevalent over Southeast China, the Tibetan Plateau (TP), Northeast China, and the southern China, respectively. Temporally, the frequency of these four types of events peaks progressively from May to August, and the PEPEs with longer movement distances tend to occur in the early morning. In terms of large-scale circulation patterns, long-distance eastward-moving PEPEs are favored by the southwestward extension of the Western Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH); short-distance eastward-moving PEPEs are associated with a meridional dipole of geopotential height anomaly around the TP; the northeastward-moving type is likely influenced by a wave-train circulation pattern in high latitudes; westward-moving PEPEs occur more frequently when the WPSH extends northwestward. These findings provide a comprehensive climatology of PEPE movement and highlight distinct circulation controls, which may aid in the prediction of moving extreme precipitations.

papers.title: High-resolution soil moisture forecasts for drought early warning in Germany
papers.authors: Najafi, H., Boeing, F., Thober, S., Rakovec, O. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Drought early warning increasingly relies on high-resolution monitoring, but the skill of daily soil moisture forecasts at lead times of 1–2 weeks driven by real-time meteorological ensembles has rarely been evaluated directly against an operational drought-monitoring framework. The Hydrological Sub-seasonal Forecasting System (HS2S) extends an established national drought-monitoring framework into high-resolution probabilistic soil moisture forecasts up to two weeks ahead for Germany at 0.015 625 ∘ resolution. We evaluated a daily-initialised HS2S configuration using the 51-member real-time forecast ensemble from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts during the exceptionally dry spring and summer of 2025 against the operational, model-based German Drought Monitor (GDM), generated within the same mesoscale Hydrologic Model (mHM) framework using observation-based meteorological forcing. The assessment combined drought onset/recovery transition diagnostics with probabilistic (Brier skill score) and categorical verification against an initialised two-state Markov persistence benchmark, and continuous verification against an mHM soil moisture climatology. HS2S reproduced the timing and mean magnitude of GDM-indicated drought onset and recovery. It showed positive probabilistic skill relative to the initialised Markov benchmark and positive continuous skill relative to the 1950–2017 mHM climatology at both lead times. For moderate drought ( SMI 0.20 ), the critical success index improved by 15.0 and 15.5 percentage points at lead weeks 1 and 2, respectively. The probability of detection of GDM-indicated drought was 95% and 89% at the same lead times. Given HS2S and the GDM share the same mHM–Soil Moisture Index framework and initial states, the verification is model-consistent and evaluates skill in anticipating the GDM-indicated drought state rather than validating absolute soil moisture accuracy. The added value of real-time meteorological forecasts relative to historical meteorological sequences was not assessed. Within this operationally relevant framework, HS2S showed forecast skill up to two weeks ahead during the 2025 drought, highlighting the potential of high-resolution probabilistic soil moisture forecasts to complement national drought monitoring with forward-looking information.

papers.title: When Scientific Uncertainty is Linked to Lower Information Avoidance: Motivational Pathways to Public Engagement With Climate Risk Information
papers.authors: Hong, S.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how scientific uncertainty is associated with both appetitive and aversive motivations, as well as its direct and indirect associations with risk information avoidance (RIA). Drawing on Liu and Chen's (2026) appetitive–aversive motivational framework, based on the Planned Risk Information Avoidance (PRIA) model, we investigate how uncertainty relates to information avoidance through risk perception, perceived information insufficiency, informational efficacy, information overload, information‐seeking norms, and negative emotions. Using structural equation modeling with a US adult sample, the findings indicate that scientific uncertainty is negatively associated with information avoidance and is linked to multiple motivational pathways. Specifically, higher scientific uncertainty is associated with greater risk perceptions and information insufficiency, and with lower levels of information overload, which in turn correspond to reduced avoidance intentions. These findings provide insight into the role of scientific uncertainty in shaping RIA, highlighting its potential to reduce avoidance in the context of climate change.

papers.title: All IPCC AR6 regions are close to their 1.5 °C- and 2 °C-equivalent warming limits
papers.authors: Tong Li, Francis W. Zwiers, Xuebin Zhang, Qiaohong Sun
papers.abstract: Global temperatures have averaged 1.2 °C above pre-industrial levels over the past decade, yet regional warming patterns and remaining warming budgets under Paris Agreement limits remain uncertain owing to insufficient historical observations. Here we quantify and attribute warming across all IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) regions since pre-industrial times using a Bayesian framework combining multi-model simulations with observations, enabling robust estimates in data-sparse regions. Regional warming is already pronounced. By 2025, attributed regional warming had reached about 90–94% of the levels expected at 1.5 °C global warming and 65–76% of those expected at 2 °C. Attribution confidence is the highest in tropical regions, including much of Africa, where low internal variability enables robust results. Attributed warming is the greatest in northern high-latitude regions, exceeding 2.5 °C. Greenhouse gases dominate, partially offset by aerosol cooling. These results reveal that current warming is already indistinguishable from a 1.5 °C world, highlighting the shared urgency of adaptation across all regions. Climate targets are set for global temperatures, but what they mean regionally is less clear. Here the authors quantify the amount of human-induced warming in individual IPCC regions and find that, by 2025, they had reached 90–94% (65–76%) of their expected warming levels at the 1.5 °C (2 °C) global warming thresholds.

papers.title: Governing wildfire insurance under mortgage constraints: an availability-affordability-capacity framework with decision-oriented evaluation for California, 2018–2024
papers.authors: Lu Chao, XiaoXi Ma, Sun ShuiMiao
papers.abstract: Abstract Catastrophe insurance economics has long recognized that disaster insurance markets fail on both sides of the market, with households under-insuring low-probability high-consequence risks and insurers unable to diversify or price correlated catastrophe exposure. The resulting debate between risk-based pricing and affordability has been conducted almost entirely within single margins: demand studies treat coverage as an annual household choice, supply studies treat insurer withdrawal as a market outcome, and government-intervention studies treat residual instruments as add-ons to a functioning market. This paper argues that all three assumptions are inadequate for mortgaged homeowners in wildfire-exposed regions, where coverage is a continuing contractual condition and the residual market is capacity-constrained. It develops an availability-affordability-capacity framework in which the offer margin, the budget margin, and the capacity margin are determined jointly under a mortgage covenant, and it evaluates the framework with a calibrated structural model estimated on a county panel for California from 2018 to 2024. The theoretical contribution is a formal allocation model that derives when each margin binds and when policy instruments are substitutes or complements, and a decomposition showing why the risk-pricing-versus-affordability debate persists: the sign of the joint response depends on local income densities and capacity binding, so it is ambiguous in theory and must be resolved empirically. The empirical contribution includes a temporal holdout, a cross-region transfer to Oregon and Colorado, and a decision-oriented evaluation protocol that shows how predictive accuracy and decision outcomes can rank pricing regimes differently. A full-profile scan of the 6,185 articles published in this journal between 2015 and 2025, together with a coded synthesis of the 135 articles on fire hazards and insurance governance, documents that the fragmentation the framework predicts is visible in the journal's own output. The model reproduces the observed trajectory of the California FAIR Plan share in-sample and tracks it out-of-sample through 2023, identifies the 2024 acceleration as a decision-relevant signal, and shows that capacity rationing becomes binding under sustained supply tightening.

papers.title: Development and validation of a Lake Michigan compound flood model
papers.authors: Benjamin Nelson-Mercer, Jeremy D. Bricker, Michael Notaro et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Compound flooding threatens communities along the coastline of the Laurentian Great Lakes, where intense rainfall and high lake levels can occur simultaneously, creating large flood impacts. Understanding the extent and impact of these floods is important for planning and assessing risk in areas with vulnerable populations and infrastructure. To increase knowledge of Great Lakes compound flooding, this study develops and tests a coupled hydrodynamic-wave model for the Great Lakes, using Berrien County, Michigan and Milwaukee, Wisconsin as test cases. The model simulates a set of historical compound flood events that occurred during a period of high Lake Michigan levels. While hydrodynamic models offer important insights into​ flood risk, evaluating their performance is often challenging due to a lack of in situ data of flooding events. To overcome this challenge, this study incorporates location-specific feedback from local experts to guide model development and validate the modeled inundation. Data shared by these experts include​s geolocated images taken during a flood event as well as feedback provided through public participatory GIS (PPGIS) that are used to qualitatively and quantitatively validate the compound flood model’s performance. This showcases useful techniques for flood model validation that can be applied to other data-scarce areas and events.

papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: Catastrophe-insurance research has established that availability, affordability, mortgage finance, and public backstops are connected, but it seldom solves the resulting allocation when the residual market can itself bind. We develop an availability-affordability-capacity framework for mortgaged homeowners and evaluate it with a structural California model for 2018–2024. The four structural parameters are fitted jointly to independently constructed FAIR Plan ratios for 2018–2021 only; 2022–2023 is a true temporal holdout, and 2024 is an estimate. Calibration MAE and RMSE are 0.0770 and 0.0779% points; holdout MAE and RMSE are 0.1796 and 0.2193 points. In 2023 the allocation is 79.818% voluntary coverage, 3.444% residual coverage, and 16.739% model-implied force-placement exposure. Exposure is 2.73% points below its 2018 level and 0.61 points above its 2021 level; the post-2021 movement is modest and does not restore the earlier level. Across nine predeclared open-bin mappings, 2023 exposure spans 15.529–18.081%. Counterfactuals, the affordability surface and the decision grid are recomputed from the same structure. The 2023 baseline covenant-feasible coverage is 83.261%; an $850 voucher raises it to 84.798%, whereas a supply tightening lowers it and makes the 6% capacity bound bind. All four weighting schemes in the decision grid select the lower boundary lambda = 1.6, so we report a boundary choice and do not claim an interior optimum. Florida Citizens supplies a pre-specified directional contraction test, and Texas TWIA supplies a statutory funding-waterfall stress map. The third state is a modelled exposure to lender-protection action, not an observed servicer action or uninsured rate. The literature layer is supported by a query-logged audit: 28 executions, 2,643 records retrieved, 1,545 unique candidates screened, and 402 records included. The contribution is narrowed to a capacity-constrained residual-market allocation with decision-oriented evaluation.

To overcome this challenge, this study incorporates location-specific feedback from local experts to guide model development and validate the modeled inundation. Data shared by these experts include​s geolocated images taken during a flood event as well as feedback provided through public participatory GIS (PPGIS) that are used to qualitatively and quantitatively validate the compound flood model’s performance. This showcases useful techniques for flood model validation that can be applied to other data-scarce areas and events.

papers.title: Understanding the role of rail transit in shaping urban population density models: A dual-level analysis of Chinese cities at city and station levels
papers.authors: Haoyu Hu, Jianfa Shen, Hengyu Gu et al.
papers.abstract: Urban rail transit is an integral component of urban morphology, which plays a role in guiding the spatial distribution of urban populations. Understanding this dynamic is essential for rational urban planning to mitigate uncontrolled urban sprawl and promote sustainable transit-oriented development. While urban population density models are widely used to quantitatively capture these spatial distribution patterns, the existing literature lacks comprehensive studies integrating city-level and station-level analyses to elucidate how rail transit networks associate with these density dynamics. Using grid-level population data from China’s seventh national census, this study estimates a generalised urban population density model for cities with operational rail transit. We employ XGBoost models to investigate the statistical associations between rail transit features and population density patterns at both the overarching city level and the localised station level. Within the generalised model, we define two key parameters: the Peak Location Index (D), which determines the peak position of the population density curve; and the Decay Radius (r 0 ), which reflects the flatness of overall population density decay. The results show that the population coverage and scale expansion contribute to D and r 0 separately. Station-level studies further corroborate that metro stations are more conducive to population uplift in places far from the city centre. Apart from the effects of built environment factors, station location within the network and years of operation also exhibit notable predictive importance regarding population density. This sheds light on the need for policymakers to rationalise rail transit planning as a tool for urban population redistribution.

papers.title: Should we predict wildlife–vehicle collision hotspots from road and landscape characteristics?
papers.authors: Federica Castagnoli, Emanuele Fior, Valeria Rossi, Stefano Leonardi
papers.abstract: Wildlife-vehicle collisions (WVCs) represent a global challenge for human safety and biodiversity conservation. This study investigates the environmental and road characteristics that influence WVC risk, using the province of Parma (Northern Italy) as a representative case study. We analysed 693 collision events recorded between 2013 and 2018, most of which involving roe deer (Capreolus capreolus, 86%) and wild boar (Sus scrofa, 10%). Spatial and temporal analysis revealed how collisions are not randomly distributed, peaking on busy major roads where high average speeds coincide with fragmented landscapes. Higher collision frequency was observed near croplands and riparian corridors, particularly at the peri-urban interface. Temporal patterns confirm that most WVCs occur during crepuscular and nocturnal hours, aligning with peak ungulate activity. Our research identifies critical road segments from environmental predictors, providing a robust spatial baseline to identify priority locations for mitigation measures, such as wildlife underpasses and road signage, to enhance both habitat permeability and drivers' safety.

papers.title: Chemical pretreatments for odorant emission control of poultry byproducts and dynamic reactions during soil application
papers.authors: Edward T. Drabold, Will Neville, Anna Mayes et al.
papers.abstract: Presently, many meat byproducts are land-applied as fertilizer. Expansion of this practice has led to significant public outcry over odorous emissions. Unlike biosolids or manure application, which have been well studied, land application odor control for mostly undigested meat byproducts has received little attention. In the case of the poultry industry, the most land-applied meat byproduct is dissolved air flotation (DAF) solids. In this work, chemical pretreatments, including addition of agricultural lime, quick lime, acid, or oxidizers were considered for DAF solids odorant emission control of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOC odorant emissions were quantified by analytical means (GC/MS), not human perception. The application method for quick lime was also considered - including pre-mixing versus surface application of quick lime after DAF solids. These experiments were conducted in controlled mesocosms with real soil, environmental perturbation to understand moisture effects, and were performed until odor extinction (∼200 h) to capture longer-term behavior. The results revealed that pre-mixed quick lime (pH of 12) removed volatile fatty acid (VFAs) emissions below detection without worsening sulfur-organic emissions (a common issue with liming). Meanwhile, agricultural lime delayed VOC odorant emissions and other chemical treatments either increased emissions or had no significant effect. A follow-up mechanistic study determined that VFA volatilization in mesocosm systems was likely due to percolation of liquid from DAF solids and acidification in the soil. Complete mixing with the acidic soil amplified odorant emissions. This study provides important insights into mechanisms that lead to malodors in meat byproduct land application.

papers.title: Nanocellulose-sewage sludge ash composite beads as sustainable sorbents for advanced wastewater treatment
papers.authors: Praveena Pachaiappan, Laura Torrent, Bruno Valentim et al.
papers.abstract: Herein, we report the formulations of composite beads to be used as adsorbent materials for water treatment, based on acid-treated sewage sludge ash (ASSA), obtained from mono-combustion, combined with polysaccharide-based biopolymers (chitosan, carboxymethylcellulose and TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanofibers (TOCNF)), with glutaraldehyde (GA) or sodium alginate (SA) as cross-linkers. The resulting materials were characterized by SEM-EDS, both on the surface and in the inner section, and by tomography, highlighting the homogeneous distribution of ashes in the polysaccharide matrix and a highly porous network. The composites were tested as adsorbents for water treatment via batch adsorption experiments to evaluate their removal capacity for textile dyes and heavy metals. Comparative analyses revealed that beads reinforced with polymeric networks exhibited markedly higher adsorption efficiencies than corresponding blank formulations and raw ash-based sorbents. Notably, composite beads fabricated with TOCNF, SA, and ASSA displayed enhanced adsorption performance and mechanical integrity. Adsorption performances were described by the Langmuir isotherm model, indicating monolayer adsorption on uniform sites, whereas pseudo-second-order kinetic fits suggested chemisorption-dominated processes. Overall, the TOCNF-SA-ASSA composite beads demonstrate superior adsorption efficiency and operational robustness across multiple pollutant classes, underscoring their potential for advanced water treatment.

papers.title: Cyanobacterial biomass pretreatment strategies enhance biogas production and alter the anaerobic microbial community
papers.authors: Yixin Yan, Qingyu Shang, Nikoletta Tsiarta et al.
papers.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms pose severe environmental challenges in surface waters on a global scale. Although mechanical harvesting is an effective bloom mitigation strategy, sustainable utilization of the harvested biomass remains a major challenge. Anaerobic digestion (AD) offers an attractive valorisation alternative; however, relatively low methane yields limit its practical application. This study evaluated the effects of four pretreatment methods (grinding, ultrasonication, thermal, and thermochemical) on the AD performance of two bloom-forming cyanobacteria ( Aphanizomenon flos-aquae and Microcystis aeruginosa ), focusing on cell morphology, methane production and microbial community composition. Biomethane potential assays showed that ultrasonication produced the highest methane yields for both species (308.42 ± 37.67 and 376.95 ± 13.96 mL CH 4 g −1 VS for A. flos-aquae and M. aeruginosa , respectively), while grinding achieved comparable performance for A. flos-aquae , reflecting its filamentous morphology. In contrast, the colonial structure and glycocalyx of M. aeruginosa reduced the effectiveness of grinding while favouring ultrasonication and thermal pretreatments. Lower methane yields were observed at the higher organic loads assessed, suggesting substrate overloading under the tested experimental conditions. Optical microscopy demonstrated distinct species-dependent morphological responses to pretreatment, while microbial analysis revealed shifts in the relative abundance of bacterial and archaeal taxa associated with AD. These microbial observations indicate correlations between pretreatment, community composition and methane production. Overall, pretreatment enhanced methane yields by up to 94.8% compared with untreated biomass, demonstrating the importance of selecting pretreatment strategies according to cyanobacterial biomass characteristics to improve AD performance.

papers.title: Advancing resilient and sustainable project portfolio management
papers.authors: Niloufar Bagherifam, Robert Moehler
papers.abstract: Environmental disruptions, economic volatility, digital transformation, resource constraints, and increasing sustainability pressures have fundamentally reshaped the strategic role of project portfolio management (PPM). As organizations seek to balance long-term value creation with adaptability under uncertainty, resilience and sustainability have become critical portfolio capabilities. Despite growing scholarly interest, research in this area remains fragmented across project management, sustainability, strategic management, and risk management, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its intellectual development. This study presents a comprehensive bibliometric, science mapping, and thematic synthesis of resilient and sustainable PPM research published between 2006 and 2026. Following a PRISMA-guided screening process, 277 journal articles were retrieved from the Scopus database and analysed using bibliometric performance analysis, bibliographic coupling, country collaboration, and keyword co-occurrence techniques. The findings reveal a marked acceleration of research after 2020 and identify three major knowledge domains shaping the field: portfolio decision analytics, risk, uncertainty and portfolio resilience, and strategic portfolio adaptation. The review also demonstrates a conceptual shift from traditional portfolio optimisation towards adaptive governance, resilience, sustainability, and data-driven portfolio decision-making. By integrating fragmented research into a coherent intellectual structure, the study advances theoretical understanding of resilient and sustainable PPM, identifies key research gaps, and proposes a future research agenda. The findings further provide portfolio managers and policymakers with evidence-based insights for designing more adaptive, resilient, and sustainable project portfolios in increasingly uncertain environments.

papers.title: A bottom-up social cost of carbon for Latin America: Municipality-level heat-mortality damage functions from 30 million daily death records
papers.authors: Fernando Antonio Ignacio González
papers.abstract: Abstract Temperature–mortality response functions have been quantified across many climate zones, but for most of the developing world they have not been translated into country-specific economic damages at sub-national resolution. This study estimates bottom-up mortality social costs of carbon (SCC) for five Latin American countries at municipality resolution. We assemble 30 million daily death records across 10,214 municipality-equivalent units in Brazil, Mexico, Chile, Ecuador and Peru (2000–2023) and merge them with the ARCO-ERA5 reanalysis sampled at every unit centroid. Country-specific Poisson exposure–response functions, estimated separately by country with municipality, year, month and day-of-week fixed effects, recover same-day heat-mortality semi-elasticities of 10.9% (Brazil) and 13.0% (Mexico) at a daily maximum temperature of 35 °C or above, relative to a 20–25 °C reference. Translating these functions along the SSP2-4.5 warming path, with the transient climate response to cumulative emissions, an income-driven attenuation of the response, a value-of-statistical-life path that rises with projected income, and population ageing, yields central mortality SCCs of about USD 0.5/tCO₂ in Brazil and USD 0.3/tCO₂ in Mexico at a 2% discount rate, with a small negative value for cool-climate Chile and near-zero values for Ecuador and Peru. These bottom-up, mortality-only estimates are a fraction of full-system country-level SCCs but share their cross-country ordering and signs, and the underlying damage functions imply a substantial annual heat-mortality burden that the sparse regional evidence in global assessments does not capture.

papers.title: Assessing demand-side policy impacts on US urban passenger transport
papers.authors: Xiangwen Fu, Christoph Bertram, Page G. Kyle
papers.abstract: Abstract Demand-side policies could significantly mitigate energy use and carbon emissions of urban passenger transport. However, previous integrated assessment modeling studies often failed to fully evaluate their mitigation potential in the absence of explicit representation of urban transport dynamics. Here we adjust the global integrated assessment model GCAM to disaggregate passenger transport in the US region into the urban and inter-city subsectors. We analyze the impacts of transformative demand-side policies on US urban passenger transport service demand, mode share, energy use, and carbon emissions. We consider six demand-side policies (compact urban development , speed limit, shared mobility, remote working, fuel tax, and congestion fee) as well as a technology policy of vehicle electrification. We find that all demand-side policies could collectively reduce urban transport energy use and carbon emissions by approximately 60% from the baseline in 2050 by shifting and reducing transport demand. We also find that demand-side policies could deliver strong synergies with electric vehicle (EV) deployment. Under ambitious EV deployment, although most direct urban passenger transport emissions are mitigated, electricity demand would increase by 718 TWh from 2021 to 2050, as much as 16% of current US total electricity consumption. A full portfolio of demand-side policies could limit the increased electricity use for urban transport to 299 TWh in 2050, providing substantial benefits for energy savings. Our study shows that demand-side policies and vehicle electrification can be complementary in achieving decarbonization and other sustainability goals.

papers.title: Biases and predictability limits of Northern Hemisphere extratropical cyclones in subseasonal prediction systems
papers.authors: Li, S., Yang, J., Liu, A., Lu, M. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Subseasonal prediction of Northern Hemisphere extratropical cyclones (ETCs) is critical for anticipating associated weather extremes, yet biases and predictability limits of ETC activity in current forecast systems remain insufficiently quantified. Here, using hindcasts from ten state-of-the-art subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction systems within a Lagrangian tracking framework, we uncover a common and pervasive bias: the multi-model ensemble consistently predicts fewer and weaker cyclones at a one-month lead, underestimating frequency by 10%–18% and intensity by approximately 13%, with more pronounced frequency deficits exceeding 26% specifically for winter bomb cyclones. These biases are dynamically driven by misrepresented meridional temperature gradients, which contribute to weaker and meridionally displaced upper-tropospheric jets and reduced peak baroclinic instability, thereby suppressing ETC formation and intensification. We further reveal that regional ETC frequency prediction skill during their respective peak seasons is limited to approximately 9–18 d, with substantial regional contrasts: the longest predictability horizon extends over the North Pacific, whereas the horizon is shortest over the North Atlantic. These regional differences are associated with variations in the dominant large-scale atmospheric drivers and their predictability over different regions. These findings establish an event-based benchmark for evaluating subseasonal ETC predictions and underscore key forecast bottlenecks in current S2S systems. Improving the representation of large-scale baroclinic environments and further unravelling the interactions between regional ETC activity and predictability sources will be essential for advancing reliable subseasonal predictions of ETC-related hazards.

papers.title: Victoria mode drives the strengthening of tropical Atlantic SST influence on El Niño–Southern Oscillation since the mid-20th century
papers.authors: Zheng, Y., Chen, S., Kug, J., Wang, Z. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Spring tropical North Atlantic (TNA) sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies serve as an important precursor of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) development in the following winter. The influence of TNA SST on ENSO has strengthened significantly since the mid-20th century, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Using large-ensemble simulations, AGCM experiments, and the PCMCI algorithm, we demonstrate that the North Pacific Victoria Mode (VM) is the key modulator of the recent enhancement of TNA SST influence on ENSO. Since the mid-20th century, the North Pacific climate state has shifted toward the negative VM phase, strengthening northeasterly trade winds and enhancing wind–evaporation–SST (WES) feedback over the subtropical northeastern Pacific. This background change amplifies the subtropical Pacific SST response to TNA-induced atmospheric anomalies, facilitating their subsequent extension into the tropical Pacific through WES feedback and ultimately modulate ENSO development via tropical air–sea interaction. Our results reveal that decadal variation in the North Pacific climate system substantially modulates the tropical Atlantic–ENSO teleconnection.

papers.title: HydroSPI-ARX for explainable multi-scale drought early warning over Türkiye from ERA5 and ERA5-Land reanalyses
papers.authors: Ertuğrul Gül
papers.abstract: Abstract Machine-learning drought studies typically regress a smooth, autocorrelated index at single stations and report near-perfect fits. Temporal leakage is rarely controlled, and the skill the index already carries in its own history is rarely separated out. Here we present HydroSPI-ARX, an autoregressive and explainable framework for drought early warning over Türkiye. It recasts the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) as a leakage-controlled, lead-resolved classification target built from ERA5 and ERA5-Land hydroclimatic fields. Five drought targets are evaluated at leads of one, three, six and twelve months, with feature selection and scaling recomputed inside every training fold. The moderate-or-worse warning reaches a macro-F1 of 0.853 one month ahead, 0.794 at three months and 0.709 at six months. At twelve months it falls to 0.486, where no configuration retains skill. Naive persistence is ahead at one month; against it the framework gains 0.038 macro-F1 at three months and 0.066 at six, with year-block bootstrap intervals that exclude zero. Against a per-cell linear autoregression on the index's own memory, the gain is measurable only at six months (0.043, 95% interval 0.010 to 0.078). Exogenous hydroclimatic fields add 0.007 at one month and nothing beyond. Skill is therefore carried by the multi-scale memory of the index, and the learned model earns its place at the six-month horizon. Scoring the same held-out forecasts against station-derived labels lowers agreement (Cohen's kappa of 0.30, 0.26 and 0.21 at one, three and six months). The ranking of the forecasts survives, so the advantage is not an artefact of verifying against the same reanalysis. ERA5 and ERA5-Land are equivalent within a margin of 0.02 macro-F1 set in advance, and a model trained without a climate zone still forecasts inside it. A Mann-Kendall analysis shows rising three-month drought frequency over 1981 to 2025.

papers.title: Scale-aware emergent constraints on Tibetan Plateau warming: contrasting global and regional predictors
papers.authors: Wang, J., Du, J., Wang, C., Dong, W. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Emergent constraints are increasingly used to reduce uncertainty in regional climate projections by exploiting relationships across models between observable historical predictors and projected changes. However, the choice of historical window and predictor scale can strongly affect constraint performance. Using the Tibetan Plateau (TP), a region of complex terrain, as a testbed, we compare two widely used predictors for constraining future TP warming: large-scale global mean surface air temperature (GSAT) and regional TP surface air temperature (TPSAT). We show that GSAT-based constraints are sensitive to the temporal evolution of external forcing and are strongest for windows beginning around 1980, consistent with the differing historical effects of greenhouse gases and aerosols. In contrast, TPSAT-based constraints generally become stronger with longer windows, indicating that extended records help suppress internal variability and better reveal the regional forced signal. At the local scale, GSAT performs better in lower-elevation regions, whereas TPSAT is more skillful over high-elevation and topographically complex areas where regional process-related signals, including cryosphere-related feedbacks, may be more important. Motivated by this spatial contrast, we develop a scale-aware constraint framework that selects the locally preferred predictor at each grid point and reduces projection uncertainty relative to either single-predictor approach over large parts of the Plateau. These findings highlight the importance of scale-aware observational constraints and may inform constrained projections in other high-elevation and topographically complex regions.

papers.title: How intermittent piped water supplies impact households and coping strategies: a systematic review
papers.authors: Broyles, L., Chavarria, K., Weston, S., Amankwaa, G. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract More than a billion people globally use a piped water system that is an intermittent water supply (IWS), where water is often unavailable from the network. Previous reviews have summarized relationships between IWS, water quality, human health risks, and coping costs. Yet, beyond these documented impacts, IWS bears additional—often invisible—burdens on users comprising both financial and non-financial costs and social and health burdens. We conducted a systematic review to document these burdens by searching databases for publications that described human impacts of IWS and coping or adaptive management strategies at the household or individual level. We used a novel codebook of coping strategies and adaptive management to synthesize 140 studies meeting our inclusion criteria conducted in 36 countries between 1994–2023. The most frequently reported impacts were increased household spending, poor water quality, time lost managing water, livelihood disruptions, and hygiene/sanitation interruptions. We also found evidence of links between IWS and respiratory infections, vector-borne diseases, dietary changes, physical strain and injuries, dehydration, sleep disruption, psychosocial stress, and interpersonal violence. The most common coping strategies were related to water storage, purchasing, and acquisition costs. Unpredictable IWS was most commonly linked to a small set of household impacts. This review demonstrates that the impacts of IWS on households are more diverse than previously synthesized and highlights the importance of interdisciplinary work to support sustainable solutions that mitigate adverse household impacts of IWS systems.

papers.title: Mapping climate change research: a bibliometric and topic modelling analysis
papers.authors: Authors not listed
papers.abstract: Climate change research has expanded at an unprecedented pace, generating a vast and fragmented body of scholarship that often obscures broader intellectual patterns and critical gaps. This study employs a large-scale bibliometric analysis combined with Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modelling to map the field’s intellectual structure and evolution. Analyzing 346,589 peer-reviewed articles from the Web of Science, the research proceeds in two stages. First, an analysis of the entire corpus identifies 17 consolidated research patterns, synthesized into six thematic clusters: Earth System Dynamics & Modelling; Ecosystem Resilience, Biodiversity & Carbon; Human Behavior, Vulnerability & Perceptions; Governance, Policy & Institutional Responses; Technological Innovation & Methodological Development; and Regional & Urban Climate Research. Second, a focused analysis of recent literature (2020–2024) reveals nine emerging trends, highlighting a shift towards urban infrastructure, biodiversity dynamics, compound risks, and the socio-technical dimensions of decarbonization. The findings illustrate both the consolidation of established domains and the diversification of new priorities. By providing a systematic map of the climate change research landscape, this study contributes to a more integrated and actionable research agenda, helping to inform effective and equitable global responses to the climate crisis.

papers.title: Effects of climate change on hydrogeological hazard: the case of the Niscemi landslides (Southern Sicily, Italy)
papers.authors: Mónica Bini, Marco Luppichini
papers.abstract: Abstract This study analyzes precipitation variability and the hydrometeorological conditions associated with extreme hydrogeological events in the Niscemi area (southern Sicily), combining historical series (1885–2020), ERA5 data, and future projections of rainfall intensity. The comparison between the hydrogeological events of October 12, 1997, and January 26, 2026 highlights how such events can develop through different hydrometeorological configurations, yet are both preceded by high soil moisture conditions, confirming the key role of antecedent precipitation and its temporal distribution. The climatic analysis shows that cumulative precipitation does not exhibit a significant linear trend but is strongly modulated by Euro-Mediterranean atmospheric circulation, with significant negative correlations with EA (ρ = -0.74) and MOI (ρ = -0.66), and more moderate correlations with NAO and WeMO. In contrast, mean rainfall intensity shows an increasing trend over time and is only weakly correlated with the indices, with a significant relationship observed only with WeMO (ρ = -0.34). The intensification is also associated with synoptic configurations characterized by positive NAO. Projections obtained using a SARIMAX model, forced with SSP scenarios, indicate a progressive increase in rainfall intensity throughout the 21st century, reaching up to approximately 40% under high-emission scenarios. Overall, the results highlight that extreme hydrogeological events arise from the interaction between atmospheric circulation variability, thermodynamic conditions, and antecedent rainfall conditions, emphasizing the need for integrated approaches to risk assessment in a climate change context.

papers.title: Multi-scale modeling of continent-wide tracking data confirms the importance of landscape mosaics for the European wildcat
papers.authors: María Alejandra Cuentas Romero, Julian Oeser, Matteo Luca Bastianelli et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Context Land use change is a major threat to the persistence of wildlife in human-dominated landscapes, making the knowledge of the amount and spatial configuration of suitable habitat essential for conservation. The European wildcat ( Felis silvestris ) currently persists in fragmented populations and faces ever increasing human pressure. Objectives We modeled and mapped suitable wildcat habitats at the continental scale, to identify opportunities and constraints for its conservation. Methods We compiled a large telemetry dataset comprising 200 wildcats across Europe and developed multi-scale habitat suitability models using Maxent. Habitat selection was analyzed at two hierarchical levels: home-range placement within the wider landscape and selection within the established home ranges. Results At both levels, wildcats selected broadleaved forests, mixed forests, and grasslands, while avoiding landscapes dominated by large continuous forests. For home-range placement, they preferred lower terrain ruggedness and less intensive agriculture. Within the home ranges, wildcats selected forest edges and small woody features. Conclusions Our results highlight the importance of heterogeneous forest–grassland mosaics habitats. More than half of the predicted suitable habitat occurred outside protected areas, highlighting the need for effective conservation strategies beyond their borders. Predictions of suitable areas should, however, be interpreted cautiously in regions where environmental conditions extend beyond those represented in the calibration data. By providing the first continental-scale habitat suitability map based on a large European telemetry dataset, our study offers a spatial foundation for identifying conservation priorities and supporting the long-term connectivity and recovery of wildcat populations.

papers.title: A decision support framework for climate-oriented coastal wetland restoration through process-based ecosystem modeling and optimization
papers.authors: Vsevolod A. Bohaienko, Fasma Diele, Carmela Marangi et al.
papers.abstract: Wetland restoration is increasingly recognized as a nature-based climate solution, but effective planning requires balancing nonlinear ecological responses with economic and implementation constraints. We propose a conceptual and computational framework for climate-oriented coastal wetland restoration that embeds process-based ecosystem modeling within restoration optimization. Restoration strategies are represented as portfolios combining discrete intervention choices with continuous decisions on implementation intensity and spatial allocation. A vertically resolved ecohydrological model simulates soil organic carbon dynamics and decomposition-driven CO$_2$ and CH$_4$ emissions, allowing environmental outcomes to arise from the interaction between restoration decisions and ecosystem processes.The framework is illustrated through a benchmark analysis and an application to the Ebro Delta. The benchmark shows that alternative objective specifications select distinct interior and corner solutions from the same ecological trade-off. In the Ebro Delta application, imposing a budget constraint reallocates restored area from the deep-rooted vegetation type toward the less expensive shallow-rooted type, while maintaining high vegetation densities and compliance with the methane target, although the CO$_2$ target is exceeded. Global sensitivity analysis identifies the density and spatial allocation of the deep-rooted vegetation type as the main drivers of restoration performance.The results show that restoration outcomes depend not only on total vegetation cover but also on portfolio composition and implementation intensity. The proposed framework provides a flexible methodology for integrating process-based ecological models into restoration planning under alternative environmental objectives and resource constraints.

papers.title: Maintenance matters: Insights from guidelines and practice on nature-based stormwater solutions
papers.authors: Emma Girot, Ning Ding, Ivar Annus et al.
papers.abstract: Nature-based stormwater solutions (NBSS) support urban stormwater management while providing additional ecosystem services. Their hybrid grey–green design sets them apart from conventional drainage systems requiring specific maintenance to ensure long-term performance. This study combines a global practitioner survey and a review of maintenance guidelines aiming to characterize shortcomings in NBSS management, focusing on failure mechanisms and maintenance practices. Based on 22 responses, survey results show that, in the absence of maintenance, systems are mainly affected by sediment buildup, litter, and green waste accumulation, as well as excessive vegetation growth, and invasive species. Maintenance (e.g., visual inspections, litter removal) is performed regularly, from monthly to annually, consistent with guidelines. Vegetation management typically follows a seasonal frequency (∼three months). Our review of 35 guidelines indicates that maintenance practices are very diverse and context-dependent, depending on the type of NBSS and socio-ecological-technological context, reflecting a potential barrier to mainstreaming of best practices. No universal maintenance frequency can be established as it strongly depends on NBBS and local context (e.g., climate, available resources). Systematic data collection on failures, their occurrence, and impacts is however essential to support predictive local maintenance strategy.

papers.title: Bismuth-based photocatalysts for sustainable water remediation and solar hydrogen generation: State-of-the-art and future directions
papers.authors: Lovedonia K. Kganyakgo, Daniel Masekela, Kwena Desmond Modibane
papers.abstract: The rapid increase in environmental pollution and global energy demand has intensified the search for sustainable technologies capable of simultaneously addressing wastewater contamination and clean fuel generation. Photocatalysis has emerged as a promising strategy because it utilizes solar energy to drive redox reactions under mild operating conditions. Among various photocatalytic materials, bismuth-based photocatalysts have attracted significant attention due to their narrow band gaps, excellent visible-light absorption, layered crystal structures, chemical stability, and tuneable electronic properties. The review discusses the structural and functional characteristics of major bismuth-based systems. Emphasis is placed on advanced modification strategies such as heterojunction construction, metal/non-metal doping, and oxygen-vacancy defect regulation, all of which significantly improve charge separation efficiency, light harvesting and surface reaction kinetics. Recent ternary and Z-scheme systems have demonstrated excellent capability for degrading organic pollutants while concurrently enhancing hydrogen production rates under visible-light irradiation. The review further analyzes the photocatalytic mechanisms governing reactive oxygen species generation, interfacial charge migration and proton reduction pathways. Despite major progress, several limitations remain, including photo-corrosion, charge recombination, low quantum efficiency and challenges in scaling laboratory results to practical reactors. Future perspectives highlight defect-controlled nanostructures, noble-metal-free cocatalysts, real wastewater applications and pilot-scale solar reactor development. Overall, bismuth-based photocatalysts offer strong potential as multifunctional materials for integrating environmental remediation with renewable hydrogen production, supporting the transition toward sustainable energy and water treatment technologies.

papers.title: Estimation of pre-existing deformations in historical masonry vaults from contemporary point clouds
papers.authors: Giulio Lucio Sergio Sacco, Chiara Calderini, Sinan Acikgoz
papers.abstract: Vaults in historical masonry structures often feature geometric distortions whose deformation history remains unknown. Understanding these deformations can support damage assessment and residual load-carrying capacity evaluation. This study presents a methodology to estimate pre-existing deformations through non-rigid registration of a reference template to surveyed point clouds. A physics-informed iterative closest point algorithm (π-ICP) which minimises normal distances while constraining elastic strain energy is developed. The template is a triangular three-noded finite element mesh; the optimal nodal displacement field is sought as a linear optimization problem solved using least-squares approach. This enables a flexible representation of undeformed geometries, allowing imposed displacements and discontinuities such as cracks. The method is evaluated on synthetic data generated through FEM simulations of a barrel vault under differential support movement and on real data of a viaduct damaged during piling works. Both applications show accurate displacements recovery and the ability to detect pre-existing and ongoing distortions.

papers.title: Simulating human-building interactions in adaptive environments: Narrative-based coordination of human and spatial agents
papers.authors: Davide Schaumann
papers.abstract: Multi-agent simulation supports occupant behavior analyses in static buildings, but rarely extends to dynamically reconfigurable environments, preventing pre-deployment evaluation of human-building interactions. This paper introduces a narrative-based framework modeling occupants and adaptive architectural systems as agents, positioning buildings as active participants rather than passive containers. A narrative formalism coordinates human and spatial agents, a visual scripting interface enables non-experts to author interaction scenarios, and modular components aim to foster usability and transfer across spatial contexts and interaction types. An exploratory, early-stage evaluation with novice architects in an academic setting modeled eight scenarios spanning multiple spatial scales and four adaptive component types using a shared component library, indicating the framework supports simulations across spatial contexts and adaptation types. Survey responses ( n = 25) suggest participants perceived it as valuable, transferable, and supportive of complex interaction scenarios. An exploratory between-cohort comparison links reduced visual scripting node counts to improved perceived template support.

papers.title: Digital technologies for enhancing collaboration in AEC projects: Systematic literature review
papers.authors: Ermias A. Amede, Anniken Karlsen, Bjørn Sørskot Andersen, Kristina Nevstad
papers.abstract: Although digital technologies are increasingly adopted in projects, limited research has explored how they may support trust, communication, commitment, collaborative problem-solving, and alignment around shared objectives in Collaborative Project Delivery Models (CPDMs)-based AEC projects. This paper addresses a gap in understanding how digital technologies enhance collaboration in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) industry. Through a systematic review of 126 peer-reviewed articles published between 2000 and 2025, this paper maps how digital technologies enhance collaboration in CPDMs. The findings trace pathways from motivators of technology adoption to digital interventions, CPDM success factors, and project outcomes, offering actionable insights for practitioners and directions for future, context-specific research.

papers.title: Limits on growth: Governing urban futures in Beijing
papers.authors: Yiqiu Liu
papers.abstract: This paper conceptualises limits on growth in Beijing, whose 2016–2035 master plan constructs a highly selective national capital for the central state by removing functions and populations deemed non-essential. Drawing on archival analysis of planning documents since 1949, extensive expert and ethnographic interviews, and multi-sited fieldwork conducted between 2017 and 2023, it develops a Lefebvrian spatio-temporal framework with three relational dimensions for analysing urban future-making. Temporal entanglements show how a historically sedimented anti-metropolis disposition is reactivated amid contemporary state recentralisation. Performative governance examines how the diagnosis of ‘big city disease’ reframes demographic and functional pressures as urban pathology, legitimising relocation and greening as therapeutic intervention. Lived futurity reveals how officials, villagers and migrants negotiate these measures through procrastination, speculation and retreat. The article theorises limits on growth as an emergent mode of Chinese statecraft in which extra-economic priorities selectively guide the production of the urban future. Situating Beijing within a wider, politically heterogeneous turn that increasingly treats demographic and territorial growth as a crisis, it reconceives urban future-making as a politics of foreclosure: not only who profits from growth, but who is permitted to remain when growth is limited by design.

papers.title: The gendered right to the city: Mediated access, urban agriculture and women’s empowerment in Kumasi
papers.authors: Mary Duah, John Boulard Forkuor, David Forkuor et al.
papers.abstract: Urban space is a vital resource for city dwellers. While literature examines the use of formal public spaces by urban residents for commerce and social activities, scholarly attention to informal agricultural spaces remains limited. This study uses a synthesis of Kabeer’s empowerment framework and Lefebvre’s right to the city to analyse women’s access to and use of urban space for agriculture in Ghana as a transformative space where gender, body and empowerment intersect. Our findings reveal that male networks serve as gatekeepers through whom women access urban space for urban agriculture. While women’s access to this social capital is empowering, it indicates that women’s right to the city and to spatial justice is mediated, achieved through relational networks and experienced as a relational right. Our findings further reveal that women appropriate these urban spaces in ways that enhance their general well-being, bodily sovereignty and promote intergenerational rights to the city for their children. By demonstrating how women’s spatial access enables agency, bodily sovereignty and the pursuit of intergenerational rights, we argue for a more nuanced understanding of empowerment and rights within informal urban contexts in the Global South.

papers.title: Geo‐Setting Risk Assessment in Eurasia: A Multidimensional Framework and Strategies
papers.authors: Zhang, J., Dong, S., Li, J., Zhao, Z.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Amid intensifying geopolitical tensions and climate‐related pressures, geo‐setting risk has become increasingly multidimensional. This analysis of geo‐setting risk in 16 Eurasian countries from 2010 to 2023, using a composite framework integrating regional geopolitical, political, economic, social, and ecological indicators, revealed marked spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Ukraine, Armenia, the Russian Federation, Georgia, and Azerbaijan were identified as high‐comprehensive‐risk countries, whereas other countries displayed distinct vulnerabilities across specific dimensions in 2023. The findings suggest that Eurasian geo‐setting risk cannot be reduced to the Russia–Ukraine conflict alone but reflects the combined influence of conflict exposure, governance conditions, economic structure, social pressure, and ecological constraints. A two‐dimensional typology linking comprehensive risk to the dominant mechanisms is proposed to support comparative risk profiling and differentiated governance discussions.

papers.title: The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
papers.authors: Bali Lee, Tom Bearpark, Oleksandr Kit et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Carbon removal markets lack a standardized, quantitative measure of permanence risk. Inspired by value at risk in financial markets, we propose carbon at risk (CaR): a probabilistic measure of the shortfall between contracted removals and realized storage at a given confidence level and time horizon. We calibrate CaR in two proof-of-concept applications: forest carbon, where Monte Carlo simulations driven by satellite fire data yield a single-project 95% CaR of more than 70% over 200 years for California, and geological storage, where simulations using the Storage Security Calculator show that the 95% CaR ranges from 0.15% (well-regulated offshore) to 17% (poorly regulated onshore). Combining technologies in a portfolio can help manage tail risk cost-effectively. The minimum cost of meeting a permanence target depends on the magnitude and correlation structure of key risk factors. CaR provides a technology-agnostic basis for risk-calibrated buffer sizing, insurance pricing and reserve-fund design, over both policy- and climate-relevant horizons.

papers.title: Quantifying the long-term evolution of post-earthquake debris-flow activity in the epicentral area of the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, China
papers.authors: Qingyun Shi, Weihua Zhang, Chuan Tang et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract The 2008 Wenchuan earthquake triggered widespread coseismic landslides and supplied large volumes of loose material on hillslopes and channels, resulting in persistent post-earthquake debris flow activity near the epicentral area. Quantifying the long-term evolution of this activity is important for geohazard assessment, but remains challenge because debris flows are jointly controlled by sediment supply, topography, and rainfall. In this study, a catchment-scale framework was developed to evaluate debris flow activity intensity in 44 catchments affected by the Wenchuan earthquake. Multi-temporal landslide inventories from 2008 to 2019 were used to calculate landslide sediment supply potential (LSSP), which integrates landslide areal density, spatial distribution indices, and channel gradient. LSSP was then combined with representative hourly rainfall intensities from documented debris flow triggering events to derive a debris flow activity intensity index (AI DF ). The results show that active landslide area decreased from 122.05 km² in 2008 to 30.55 km² in 2019, while recovery areas expanded progressively. LSSP increased sharply immediately after the earthquake and then declined over time, with a rapid decrease during 2008–2011 followed by a slower adjustment phase. Nevertheless, sediment supply in many catchments remained above the pre-earthquake level in 2019. AI DF showed an overall decline after its post-earthquake peak, although temporary increases occurred during major rainfall events. Comparison with documented debris flow events indicates that AI DF captures the main temporal pattern of observed activity. The fitted long-term trend suggests three stages of post-earthquake debris flow activity: an active period from 2008 to 2013, a recession period from 2013 to 2048, and a relatively stable period after 2048. These results indicate that debris flow activity in the Wenchuan earthquake-affected area may persist for several decades, mainly controlled by the gradual depletion and redistribution of landslide-derived sediment under rainfall forcing.

papers.title: Beyond exposure: Pathways between urban greening, nature connection and wellbeing in Australian policy frameworks
papers.authors: Rose Macaulay, Rebecca Toohey, Stéphanie Lavau, Kathryn J. H. Williams
papers.abstract: Urban greening initiatives are increasingly positioned as strategies to improve health and wellbeing in cities. While academic research has long acknowledged the role of psychological connections to nature in shaping wellbeing, it is unclear whether and how this relationship is recognised in urban greening policy. This study examines how Australian urban greening and biodiversity strategies conceptualise and evaluate wellbeing and nature connection. We conducted a structured review of 43 policy documents from state and local governments across Australia, analysing how strategies define and operationalise these concepts. We found that while strategies acknowledge multiple dimensions of wellbeing and recognise both physical and psychological connections to nature, evaluation practices focus almost exclusively on biophysical outputs of urban greening, such as canopy cover and park access. Psychological connections to nature were absent from evaluation targets, and most strategies lacked indicators assessing medium- to long-term wellbeing outcomes. This highlights a significant gap between how wellbeing and nature connection are conceptualised and how they are evaluated in practice. We provide recommendations for integrating psychological dimensions of nature connection into urban greening policy, including clearer articulation of causal pathways, consistent conceptualisation, and development of evaluation frameworks that capture both nature connection and wellbeing as measurable outcomes.

papers.title: Effects of residential garden features on biodiversity: A systematic review
papers.authors: Muriel Deparis, Mathieu Lachaise, Quentin Dutertre, Emmanuelle Baudry
papers.abstract: In the urban mosaic of habitats, residential gardens can sustain high levels of biodiversity. Although many gardeners are interested in biodiversity-friendly designs, they lack a clear overview of the available evidence to guide their choices, as the scientific knowledge about it remains dispersed. Here, we present a comprehensive synthesis of peer-reviewed articles investigating the relationship between residential garden features and biodiversity. Through a systematic search of Web of Science and Scopus, we identified 3,872 articles and retained 31 after a three-stage screening process and critical appraisal. These articles report the effects of 16 garden features on the richness and abundance of 62 taxonomic groups. Evidence was generally sparse and uneven across garden features and taxa, with many results supported by a few studies. Arthropods were highly documented, contrary to bats, amphibians, or reptiles. Index of garden heterogeneity was the most documented feature and often showed positive effects on birds, bumblebees, and butterflies. However, many studies reported non-significant or contradictory results, limiting broad generalizations. Floral resources showed the most consistent positive effects on pollinators, regardless of their nativness. Lawn area did not show clear effects. Shrub area and tree number and cover were generally beneficial for beetles, birds, earthworms, and wasps, although many other taxa appeared unaffected. Future studies should propose new protocols to study a wider range of garden features, beyond their presence and area, and provide independent replication for poorly documented taxa. Explore the tensions between garden use and biodiversity-oriented design options is also a promising line for future research.

papers.title: Recent environmental change shapes biotic homogenisation of Orthoptera and Mantodea communities in semi-dry grasslands
papers.authors: Dominik Poniatowski, Felix Maximilian Freienstein, Marco Drung et al.
papers.abstract: Semi-dry grasslands are among the most species-rich ecosystems in Europe. However, many grassland remnants are undergoing gradual habitat degradation due to climate change, atmospheric nitrogen deposition, and the relaxation or abandonment of traditional management. While declines of specialised insects have repeatedly been reported, the extent to which these drivers promote long-term community reorganisation and biotic homogenisation remains poorly understood. Using a nationwide resurvey of 221 semi-dry grassland patches across Germany, spanning two to three decades, we investigated long-term changes in Orthoptera and Mantodea communities. We quantified changes in species richness, community composition, and beta diversity, and related these patterns to major global change drivers. Despite an increase in total species richness, these communities became increasingly homogenised, as indicated by declining beta diversity. Community reorganisation was characterised by pronounced winner-loser dynamics, with highly mobile generalists and thermophilous species expanding, whereas threatened species, low-mobility habitat specialists, and species associated with High Nature Value farmland declined. Winner species richness increased particularly in warm and dry regions, under elevated atmospheric nitrogen deposition, and outside protected areas. By contrast, low-mobility habitat specialists and threatened species persisted most successfully in structurally heterogeneous habitats. High shrub cover was negatively associated with both winners and losers, indicating an overall deterioration of habitat suitability. Our findings demonstrate that environmental change does not necessarily reduce species richness but can profoundly reorganise communities through selective filtering of species. Maintaining habitat heterogeneity with appropriate management strategies is therefore crucial for buffering biodiversity loss under ongoing global change.

papers.authors: Jieshu Wang, J. Alberto Conejero, Sergio Hoyas et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping sustainability science through advances in climate modeling, ecosystem monitoring, resource management, and evidence synthesis. Yet its use also raises concerns about reliability, equity, and environmental impacts. In this Prospective, we identify four priorities for responsible AI integration: ensuring AI-supported claims are causal, transparent, and auditable; treating model selection as an environmental decision; building sustainability-focused AI infrastructure; and engaging sustainability scientists and affected communities in AI design and governance. With these safeguards, AI can enhance sustainability science while promoting equitable and environmentally responsible decision-making.

papers.title: Wave and slope thresholds for mangrove restoration and nature-based solution design
papers.authors: Jin Liu, Andrew Pomeroy, Brendan  Scott Lanham et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Globally, shorelines are experiencing widespread recession, promoting greater interest in nature-based solutions (NbSs) for coastal protection. Along tropical and sub-tropical coastlines, mangroves are among the habitat-forming species increasingly targeted for nature-based coastal protection. However, practical implementation requires tools that identify shorelines where hydrodynamic and geomorphic conditions are likely to support successful mangrove establishment and long-term persistence. This study quantifies first-order suitability envelopes (hereafter thresholds) for mangrove presence by linking wave height and bathymetric slope to observed mangrove distributions in subtropical wave-dominated barrier estuarine systems. Mangroves were most likely to be present where the 80 th percentile significant wave height ( H s ) was below 0.14 m and bathymetric slope was gentler than 0.01. Above these thresholds, the probability of mangrove occurrence decreased from approximately 23%–25% to 13%–15%, indicating strong but non-exclusive physical controls. Importantly, the probability did not decline to zero beyond these limits, suggesting that mangrove distribution is better described as a suitability threshold rather than a fixed ecological threshold. Spatial analysis indicated that approximately 26% of currently unvegetated shoreline areas in the study fell within the identified wave-slope thresholds, representing potentially suitable but unrealized mangrove habitat. These findings demonstrate that mangrove distribution is partly governed by hydrodynamic and geomorphic processes. While these potential restoration areas are identified based strictly on hydrodynamic and bathymetric thresholds, other critical drivers, such as tidal elevation, sediment supply, and salinity gradients, may further restrict suitable locations. The proposed methods of deriving thresholds in this study provide transferable, process-based criteria for identifying restoration opportunity areas and informing the design of NbSs for coastal resilience in estuarine environments.

papers.title: Evolving energy-water infrastructure strengthens drought resilience in the U.S. Northeast and Midwest
papers.authors: Hussain H. Bokhari, Charles J Vörösmarty, Stephanie Herbert, Carry Pak
papers.abstract: Abstract Strategies to strengthen regional water security will be essential for navigating a critical 21st-century environmental challenge: securing freshwater supplies against growing demands and increasingly severe climate extremes. This paper assesses the evolution of water security in the historically water-rich U.S. Northeast (NE) and Midwest (MW) to quantify their resilience to severe drought now and in the future. We develop a counterfactual framework that projects sectoral water demands based on socio-economic drivers and deconstructs the benefits of supply- and demand-side adaptations at the regional scale. During the half-century between the historic NE/MW 1960s drought and the 2012-2013 North American drought, rapid socio-economic growth held the potential to push water systems to a breaking point, rendering them unequipped to manage the impact of such severe droughts. However, this study reveals that both regions built resilience through long-term adaptations that averted potential water crises, mitigating otherwise severe summertime water stress (withdrawal-to-available supply) by factors of 2.8 (MW) and 5.6 (NE). While supply-side strategies through reservoir construction and coastal power development played a role, the driving factor has been water demand management, accounting for 83% to 92% of summertime water stress mitigations across the two regions and drought scenarios. These gains were rooted in economic and political incentives to adopt advanced thermoelectric cooling technologies and efficient industrial technologies, together with the regions’ shift from a manufacturing to service economy. Thus, our projections of increased water demand by the mid-21st century highlight a critical reality: future drought resilience will require continued investments in demand-side efficiency gains, such as water-efficient electricity production systems, to keep pace with expected socio-economic trends.

papers.title: Manage derailment risks to avoid Hothouse Earth
papers.authors: Dyke, J., Laybourn, L., Abrams, J.
papers.abstract: Abstract The risk of a ‘Hothouse Earth’ trajectory has become increasingly prominent in debates about Earth system stability and climate overshoot. Existing analyses primarily focus on biophysical feedbacks that may amplify warming beyond direct anthropogenic forcing. We argue the concept has not previously incorporated how social destabilisation lowers the effective threshold at which biophysical tipping dynamics become self-sustaining, independently of further anthropogenic forcing and so undermines the capacity for planetary stewardship. We define ‘derailment risk’ as the possibility that escalating Earth system disruption weakens the social, political, and economic conditions required to sustain mitigation, adaptation, and ecological restoration. Such risks emerge when climate impacts contribute to a wide range of challenges, including debt crises, institutional erosion, political fragmentation, supply-chain instability, and declining public support for environmental action. These reinforcing feedbacks may reduce humanity’s capacity to respond even before biophysical tipping thresholds are crossed. We therefore extend the Hothouse Earth framework by incorporating social dynamics into the Earth system stability landscape. We propose a three-stage framework for assessing and managing derailment risks: conceptual mapping of socio-biophysical feedbacks; anticipatory resilience-building interventions; responsive governance strategies for periods of escalating instability. We conclude that planetary stewardship should prioritise maintaining and expanding collective agency under worsening Earth system stress.

papers.title: Carbon prices and cooking fires: how decarbonization pathway design shapes household energy burdens
papers.authors: George, M., Clarke, L., Min, J., Pachauri, S. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Pathways reaching the same climate target can distribute household energy costs very differently across income groups. We compare 16 core mitigation pathways spanning a cost-optimal benchmark and technology, timing, effort-sharing, and demand-side designs, plus one rebound sensitivity, within a common integrated assessment framework. All core pathways remain below 2 °C and converge to approximately 1.5 °C warming by 2100, consistent with the Paris Agreement’s 1.5 °C temperature goal. We translate energy- and food-price outcomes into household energy burdens across income deciles in India and the United States using survey-informed downscaling. In 2030, cost-optimal, technology, and pace pathways are regressive in both countries, with larger burden increases for poorer deciles. In India, lower-demand pathways reduce global carbon prices and lower burdens for poorer households, whereas accelerated electrification and rapid traditional-biomass phase-out raise burdens. Historical-responsibility transfers lower burdens in India and raise them in the United States under the stylized transfer design. A conventional gross-income sensitivity preserves pathway rankings and almost all decile-level burden-change signs but roughly halves poorest-decile magnitudes in India. Accounting for food expenditure therefore reveals affordability pressures on poorer households that gross-income measures mute. Scenario design is an equity-relevant dimension of pathway assessment alongside revenue recycling.
