papers.title: Characterizing drinking-water facility exposure to historical wildfires in Northern Colorado
papers.authors: Mosher, D., Sun, G., Caldwell, P., Zhang, Y. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Wildfire increasingly threatens forested headwater watersheds that supply drinking water to downstream communities, yet current wildfire exposure assessments rarely account for inter-basin transfers (IBTs), which can expand source-water footprints beyond natural watershed boundaries and alter the hydrologic connections between fires and drinking-water intakes. Here, we developed a reproducible assessment approach to quantify historical wildfire exposure for drinking-water intakes and applied it in northern Colorado as a case study. The analysis integrated historical (1984–2024) wildfire perimeters, burn severity, subwatershed boundaries, natural hydrologic flow paths, IBT connectivity, and public water supply utility information. Across the 7,308 km 2 study area, 1895 km 2 burned (26% of the landscape), at least one fire occurred in 54 of the 90 watersheds examined, and approximately 31% of total burned area was classified as high severity. Across all 14 events studied, fires affected drinking-water systems serving an average of 344 854 people and four downstream intake facilities per event. Intake-level exposure depended not only on fire size, but also on burn severity and hydrologic connectivity. Incorporating IBTs altered the relative importance of individual subwatersheds in headwater areas in terms of their wildfire exposure on downstream intake systems. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for both natural and managed hydrologic connectivity in source-water wildfire exposure assessments and provide a basis for decision-support tools, such as Forests to Faucets, that directly link forest disturbance, water-supply infrastructure, and downstream communities.

papers.title: Democracy and income inequality moderate the impacts of protected areas
papers.authors: Coleman, E., Kashwan, P., Haque, M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Many policymakers and conservation activists promote creating terrestrial protected areas (PAs) as a central tool to preserve biodiversity and offset global carbon emissions. However, the socioeconomic consequences of PA designation remain understudied. Using an event study design, this paper estimates the causal treatment effect of creating PAs on changes in cultivated agriculture land from within PA boundaries. We examine the global population of 64 997 terrestrial PAs established 1995–2020 and evaluate temporal changes in land classified as agriculture cultivation in 5 year intervals. We find that PAs (modestly) reduce the amount cultivation within their boundaries. Then, using data on country-level income inequality and democratic institutions we estimate the treatment effect of creating PAs in countries that are less democratic and have more income inequality. We find that PAs located in places with more income inequality and less democracy significantly reduce cultivation, at a much greater rate than in countries that score higher on democracy and have less income inequality. These findings highlight the critical role of socioeconomic and political context in shaping the outcomes of PA policies. Conservation policy in nondemocratic and high economic inequality countries must create appropriate safeguards for local people.

papers.title: Consistent drivers of lightning-ignited wildfires across global boreal forests
papers.authors: Engle, B., Bratoev, I., Crowley, M., Zhu, Y. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate change is expected to change both fire susceptibility and lightning activity in global boreal forests. The mechanics governing lightning-ignited wildfire (LIW) ignition remain, however, unclear, making predictions at global boreal scale challenging. Here we examine short-term temporal impacts of weather on ignition probability using a novel dataset on LIWs in a quasi-experimental design of ignition and non-ignition lightning pairs. Specifically, our dataset is comprised of 5251 lightning pairs coupled with temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, lightning characteristics (multiplicity, polarity, peak current, and duration) and net primary productivity. We estimate the effect of these predictor variables on ignition probability across three separate models; the full boreal, open forests and closed forests. We find a clear relationship between ignition probability and temperature, relative humidity, total precipitation, and polarity. A one standard-deviation increase in temperature (∼3.3 °C) increased ignition probability by 44%–69%, while increased precipitation and relative humidity reduced ignition probability. Both temperature and precipitation were most predictive 3–8 d before lightning and the effect lasted up to 7–11 d after lightning. Positive polarity was also associated with increased ignition likelihood. Our results suggest that LIW occurrence within the global boreal is primarily driven by short-term fire weather rather than lightning characteristics alone. A projected increase in temperatures is expected to drive ignition probability in the boreal, though this may be partly offset by an increase in total precipitation.

papers.title: Public safety and congestion in Latin American smart cities: A Grey Incidence Analysis
papers.authors: Damaris Chieregato Vicentin, Gustavo Hermínio Salati Marcondes de Moraes, Walter Leal Filho et al.
papers.abstract: Everyday urban problems in Latin American cities, particularly those related to public safety and traffic congestion, have become increasingly relevant in debates on smart and sustainable urban development. This study investigates perception-based indicators of structural and technological aspects associated with more favorable perceptions regarding everyday urban problems in 12 Latin American cities, focusing on public safety and traffic congestion. The methodology employed Grey Incidence Analysis on indicators from the IMD Smart City Index 2025. The results reveal that more favorable perceptions regarding public safety are most strongly associated with lifelong learning opportunities offered by local institutions, followed by access to basic sanitation in poorer areas. In contrast, more favorable perceptions regarding traffic congestion are most strongly associated with satisfaction with public transport and the perceived contribution of ride-sharing apps to reducing congestion. Parking guidance apps and bike-sharing services show a comparatively weaker relational link to favorable perceptions regarding congestion. The study contributes to citizen-centric smart city research by showing that urban policies require problem-specific configurations: socially integrated structural interventions for public safety and coordinated transport infrastructure and digital mobility solutions for congestion.

papers.title: Estimation of Excess Inhalation Non‐Cancer and Cancer Risk From Volatile Organic Compound Mixtures in New York City Nail Salons
papers.authors: Ierardi, A., Thompson, R., Fisher, S., Anderson, K. et al.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Nail salon workers are acutely and chronically exposed to mixtures of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), yet health risks in New York City (NYC) salons have not been systematically assessed. We performed an occupational risk assessment using integrated real‐time total VOC (TVOC) monitoring and chemical‐specific sampling of 11 VOCs across five NYC salons. Median and peak exposures and their 95th percentile (upper‐bound) values were used in non‐cancer and cancer risk models using deterministic and probabilistic approaches. Deterministic non‐cancer risk modeling indicated hazard indices (HIs) were generally below the benchmark value of 1, with exceedances observed only using upper‐bound exposures in the salon with the highest VOC concentrations. The probabilistic non‐cancer assessment showed a similar pattern, with some salons having non‐negligible probabilities of HI exceedance despite median HIs below 1. Deterministic and probabilistic benzene cancer risk assessments indicated exceedances of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) de minimis benchmark under multiple exposure scenarios. Although VOC concentrations were below occupational exposure limits (OELs), incorporating exposure variability and uncertainty identified elevated non‐cancer and cancer risks under certain scenarios. Previous research has linked nail salon work to adverse health effects, including respiratory symptoms and developmental and reproductive effects, suggesting that current OELs may not adequately protect this workforce. Our results highlight the need for improved exposure limits, chemical mixture risk assessment methods, and health protections for nail salon workers.

papers.title: Incentive-compatible risk preferences and sustainable land management adoption under climate risk: Evidence from semi-arid Kenya
papers.authors: Amos Nyangira Tirra, Rose Adhiambo Nyikal, John Mburu et al.
papers.abstract: Sustainable land management (SLM) practices are widely promoted as an effective pathway for mitigating climate-induced production risks and enhancing agricultural sustainability. However, their uptake has remained low across Sub-Saharan Africa despite the associated benefits. Existing studies have primarily evaluated socio-economic and institutional determinants, with limited evidence on incentivized risk preference and loss aversion, particularly for multiple practice adoption. This gap is especially consequential in arid and semi-arid regions, where production uncertainty is high and adoption decisions are inherently risky. In South Eastern Kenya (SEK), recurrent droughts and extreme climate events have contributed to widespread food insecurity, crop losses, and livestock deaths, making adoption important for agricultural sustainability and climate resilience. Using data from 867 farm households selected through multistage sampling in semi-arid SEK, this study examines how risk preference and loss aversion are associated with SLM adoption breadth. An incentivized field experiment was employed to elicit both measures while adoption behaviour was assessed using a generalized Poisson regression model. Risk-loving farmers show greater adoption breadth than risk-averse farmers, while higher loss aversion is associated with lower adoption breadth. Locus of control, aspiration, wealth, shock exposure and crop diversity are positively associated with adoption breadth. Perceived climate-resilience benefits show a modest positive association, whereas perceived productivity and environmental-quality benefits are negatively associated. These findings highlight the relevance of behavioural heterogeneity for strategies to broaden SLM adoption in climate-vulnerable semi-arid areas.

papers.title: Quantification and characterisation of the illegal dumping of municipal waste
papers.authors: Beatriz Afonso, Graça Martinho, Joaquim Pires Pina, Mário Ramos
papers.abstract: Even in developed countries, municipal waste (MW) left outside communal containers remains a significant challenge, affecting urban hygiene. This study analysed the improper disposal of MW across three monitoring circuits, each 14 km long, representing rural inland, urban inland, and urban coastal settings, with particular attention to the pre-holiday period and the preparation of dwellings for the tourist season. A total of 128 sites were systematically monitored over three periods, recording 407 occurrences. The total estimated volume and mass of abandoned MW varied across circuits, with the urban inland circuit accounting for the highest number of new occurrences, as well as the largest estimated volumes and masses of waste. By volume, paper and cardboard packaging and bulky waste predominated, particularly in the coastal urban area. By mass, construction and demolition waste (CDW) arising from minor construction and demolition activities within private households accounted for the largest fraction. In Portugal, the management of CDW generated by such activities is the responsibility of MW management systems. Furthermore, higher per capita amounts of abandoned MW were recorded in the urban coastal area. These patterns may reflect the preparation of dwellings for the summer tourist season. The recurrence of improper waste disposal highlighted operational challenges for waste collection planning. The findings also suggest a potential role of citizen behaviour in waste abandonment. In addition, the study developed context-adjusted indicators of MW abandonment, which may support further research and inform MW management practices, particularly by helping to identify spatial patterns of waste abandonment and optimise collection strategies.

papers.title: An integrated assessment framework for comparing and enhancing flood resilience in heterogeneous floodplains
papers.authors: Thanh Phuoc Ho, Wenhan Feng, Trung Nguyen Ly et al.
papers.abstract: Climate change is intensifying flood hazards in deltas, challenging agricultural communities dependent on hydrological conditions. Flood resilience has therefore emerged as an alternative to traditional risk management. Yet, comparative resilience studies often overlook how resilience measures vary across floodplain hydrological regimes (FHRs) within a delta. This study proposes an integrated flood-resilience assessment framework integrating FHRs, including freshwater (Fresh_Fl), transitional (Transitional_Fl), and tidal (Tidal_Fl), with flood resilience capacities (FRCs) (absorptive, adaptive, and transformative). Using the Vietnamese Mekong Delta as a case study, the framework operationalizes 31 flood-resilience measures as regime-specific indicators, drawing on 357 surveys and 30 semi-structured interviews. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used to visualize broad resilience orientations, while Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis H tests identified statistically supported measure-level differences. Results show that most measures were applied and received high perceived-effectiveness scores with non-significant differences, forming a shared baseline across FHRs, whereas each FHR showed different measure emphases. Fresh_Fl was characterized by strong absorptive protection through large-scale dikes, and farmer-led low dikes were perceived more positively than in Transitional_Fl. Yet, high-dike dominance reduced the role of some adaptive measures and shifted environmental and downstream trade-offs. Additionally, Transitional_Fl and Tidal_Fl showed higher ratings for mechanization and flood utilization under variable water conditions, while government support for flood-adaptive rice was rated more positively in Fresh_Fl and Transitional_Fl. These findings support resilience planning moving beyond one-size-fits-all strategies and differentiated policy pathways considering hydrological conditions, feasibility, governance responsibilities, and maladaptation risks. The framework offers conditional decision-support logic for other flood-prone deltas.

papers.title: Layered double hydroxides functionalized electrospun recycled polyamide 6 from fishing nets: structure–property relationships for antimicrobial non-woven fabrics
papers.authors: Annafelicia Civitavecchia, Simona Sabbatini, Emiliano Laudadio et al.
papers.abstract: Plastic pollution, particularly marine plastic waste from discarded fishing nets, represents a significant environmental challenge and highlights the need for effective strategies to recover and valorize end-of-life polymers. Polyamide 6 (PA6) fishing nets are an underexploited source for the development of high-value functional materials. This work develops antimicrobial non-woven fabrics (NWFs) from recycled PA6 (rPA6) incorporating organo-modified Mg/Al layered double hydroxides (LDHs) intercalated with antimicrobial anions, namely ascorbate (ASA), ferulate (FER), salicylate (SAL), and citrate (CA), into rPA6, followed by electrospinning. The resulting nanofibrous NWFs were characterized by Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM), Fourier Transformed Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Wide Angle/Small Angle X-ray Scattering with micro-beam (μWAXS/μSAXS), thermal analysis and tested against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus. Homogeneous nanofibers were obtained and LDH incorporation preserved rPA6 chemical structure while reducing crystallinity. rPA6/LDH-FER, rPA6/LDH-ASA, and rPA6/LDH-CA, showed 96.7 to 99.9% bacterial mortality. After thermal aging at 115 °C, LDH-containing NWFs exhibited improved structural stability. These results demonstrate the feasibility of converting recycled PA6 fishing-nets into functional antimicrobial nanofibrous fabrics through LDH functionalization and electrospinning, supporting circular and sustainable applications of marine recycled polyamides.

papers.title: Spatially compounding climate extremes and environmental risk: cross-regional synchrony, spatial buffering loss, and systemic consequences
papers.authors: 朱爱辉, Dayun Zhu
papers.abstract: Abstract Spatially compounding climate extremes are increasingly recognized as a source of climate-related risk, and their risk significance depends on how synchrony affects connected systems. The critical transition occurs when cross-regional synchrony reduces support from places that would otherwise buffer one another through substitution, reserve capacity, mutual assistance or recovery support—a condition we term spatial buffering loss. This Topical Review synthesizes empirical and methodological evidence to examine how synchrony is generated, when it translates into functional loss, and what is required to assess that transition. Food production, water allocation and firefighting cooperation provide complementary settings for examining substitution, reserve and assistance functions, while the synthesis distinguishes joint exposure from support available to recipients. Atmospheric circulation, persistent weather patterns, land–atmosphere feedbacks and hydrological connectivity can organize synchrony; functional evidence determines whether that synchrony reduces compensating support and produces systemic consequences. Accordingly, credible assessment must connect event topology and joint-tail behaviour with functional exposure, an explicit compensating relation and a counterfactual estimate of support that would otherwise have remained available. By linking event organization to recipient support, the synthesis provides a functional basis for assessing spatial buffering loss across connected systems. This perspective connects the evidence to decisions about supplier diversification, reserve operation and mutual assistance.

papers.title: Is Indigenous Knowledge meaningfully represented in the IPCC AR6? A bibliometric meta-analysis
papers.authors: Ritodhi Chakraborty, Pasang Yangjee Sherpa, Eric Nost et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract In recent global climatic and environmental reports, Indigenous Knowledges (IK) are recognised as essential to comprehending social-ecological systems and multi-scalar climate-society relationships. However, IK and Indigenous Peoples (IP) continue to be mostly excluded from important and powerful processes such as the UNFCCC and the IPCC reports. In the current (AR7) cycle of the IPCC, it is important to understand whether the last cycle (AR6) meaningfully engaged with IK and IP. Here, we present a multi-tiered bibliometric analysis of the literature cited in the AR6 report (n=46,145 citations), through which we identified citations with abstracts mentioning IK (n=482). Additionally, through exploring this cluster of IK citations, we address enduring questions around disciplinary bias, geographical bias, and academic journal bias. Finally, we categorise IK citations using two indexes of equitable knowledge production. This highlights the different types of relationships (from extractive to co-productive) that guided the cited papers’ research process. Our findings highlight that despite advocacy, promises, and assurances, IK is mostly excluded from the IPCC AR6 report (1.04% of scholarly literature cited). We also call attention to the fact that biophysical sciences, elite journals, and authors from the Global North are dominant in the IK that is included. Finally, we identify some key points of intervention for AR7, which include strategic choices for chapter authors, a focus on Working Group I (climate science), and the inclusion of chapter-scale knowledge justice audits.
papers.titleKo: Is Indigenous Knowledge meaningfully represented in the IPCC AR6? A bibliometric meta-analysis

papers.title: Increasing favorability for intense tropical cyclone activity in the northern South China Sea
papers.authors: 崖丽娟, Jieyi Ou, Yongfen Zhao et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract The South China Sea (SCS) is one of the most active marginal seas for tropical cyclones (TCs) worldwide and a key region for TC hazards along the coasts of southern China, Philippines and Vietnam. However, the drivers of long-term changes in intense TC development in this region remain unclear. Here, we show that the number of TCs reaching Category 3-5 intensity has increased significantly, with more occurring in the northern SCS. This change is primarily linked to an increasing contribution of western North Pacific TCs entering through the Luzon Strait, which experience weaker land-induced weakening than those crossing the Philippine archipelago and retain greater intensity for subsequent development. After entering the SCS, reduced ocean cooling and enhanced oceanic and atmospheric conditions have increased the environmental favorability for intense TC development in the northern SCS. These results highlight the role of regional ocean-land-atmosphere interactions in reshaping where TCs reach high intensities.

papers.title: Integrating local ecological knowledge from professional fishers with environmental observations can improve the understanding, forecasting, and management of climate-sensitive jellyfish hazards
papers.authors: Seo Yeol Choi, Seok‐Hyun Youn, Kyoung Yeon Kim
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate variability is increasing the frequency and impacts of marine hazards, yet early warning systems often lack mechanisms to translate environmental signals into timely governance responses. Here, we examine how local ecological knowledge can be operationalized within a national hazard monitoring framework using jellyfish blooms as a model marine hazard. We analyzed 15 years (2010–2024) of weekly, fisher-reported observations from Korean coastal waters, focusing on Aurelia coerulea and Nemopilema nomurai. From these weekly reports, we calculated occurrence rate, defined as the percentage of respondents reporting jellyfish presence, and aggregation frequency, defined as the percentage reporting jellyfish aggregations. These indices were interpreted as operational risk indicators rather than standardized abundance estimates. Their utility was evaluated by testing temporal alignment with official national jellyfish alerts and by quantifying species-specific lead–lag structures. Distinct bloom dynamics emerged: A. coerulea formed persistent aggregations peaking from late spring to summer, whereas N. nomurai exhibited low background occurrence punctuated by abrupt mass events in late summer to autumn. Monthly sea surface temperature (SST) showed positive associations with fisher-reported occurrence and aggregation frequencies for both species (p < 0.05). Generalized Additive Models indicated a long-term weakening of A. coerulea bloom intensity and an earlier seasonal shift in N. nomurai peaks, consistent with warming-related phenological change. Alert timing closely tracked A. coerulea peaks, while N. nomurai alerts preceded peaks by 4–6 weeks, reflecting differences in life history and cross-boundary transport. By linking weekly fisher-reported bloom signals with official national jellyfish alerts, this study shows how local ecological knowledge can provide decision-relevant information for bloom timing and operational response to jellyfish hazards under changing climate conditions.

papers.title: Greenhouse gas forcing dominates the recent strengthening of North Pacific Meridional mode influence on ENSO
papers.authors: Yuqiong Zheng, Shangfeng Chen, Bin Yu et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract The North Pacific Meridional Mode (NPMM) is a key extratropical trigger of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events, and its influence on ENSO has increased markedly in recent decades, offering a pathway to improve ENSO predictability. Yet, the relative contributions of external forcings versus internal variability to this intensified influence remain uncertain. Using multi-model simulation outputs from the Detection and Attribution Model Intercomparison Project and a suite of numerical experiments, we demonstrate that greenhouse gas (GHG) forcing dominates over internal variability in driving the recent strengthening of the NPMM–ENSO connection, whereas aerosol and natural forcings have minimal impact. GHG forcing enhances the wind–evaporation–SST feedback over the subtropical North Pacific by elevating the background mean SST, which amplifies NPMM-induced westerly wind bursts over the western tropical Pacific and promotes ENSO development. Sensitivity experiments further demonstrate that GHG-induced SST increasing in the subtropical North Pacific enhances the atmospheric response associated with the NPMM. These findings reveal an important role of anthropogenic forcing in modulating the extratropical impact on ENSO and suggest potential opportunities for extending ENSO prediction lead times.

papers.title: Regional economic impacts and emission responses under solar radiation modification
papers.authors: Bjordal, J., Dijk, E., Cornec, H., Smith, A. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Solar radiation modification (SRM) has been proposed as a potential tool to limit increases in global or regional temperatures caused by anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions. While previous research has extensively examined the climate system’s response to various SRM strategies, as well as their aggregate economic consequences, the spatial distribution of economic impacts has received less attention. In this study, we use NorESM2-Disaggregated Integrated Assessment Model—an Earth System Model coupled to a high-resolution integrated assessment model—to assess the economic impacts, measured in gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, in an idealised SRM scenario where incoming solar radiation is reduced by 1%. Our results suggest that, relative to a baseline without SRM, most countries experience economic gains under SRM, with only a few countries facing negative impacts. Low-income countries tend to see the largest benefits, reducing disparities in GDP per capita across countries relative to the baseline. However, reduced damages and smaller disparities in GDP per capita are accompanied by a ‘moral hazard’ effect, in that SRM leads to higher emissions, which may in turn cause additional adverse effects not captured here. These findings highlight potential trade-offs between economic benefits, the distribution of economic impacts, and increased emissions relevant for SRM governance.

papers.title: The simultaneous slow death and persistent vitality of social infrastructure in elite neighbourhoods
papers.authors: Sharda Rozena, Rowland Atkinson
papers.abstract: This article examines the vitality of social life at street level over time in the patrician elite area of Kensington, London. We consider how luxury amenities, prime homes and high-end stores intersect with the durable presence of an everyday, working city comprising diverse social infrastructures: budget hotels, rent-controlled housing and interstitial social spaces of cafes, parks and street benches. These layers of uses and users co-exist in complex time–space configurations despite the historical and contemporary designation of the neighbourhood as an elite space. Using a range of data sources, we show how the neighbourhood contains distinct features that enable the limited and partial social engagement and hypermobility of wealthy bodies with the social life of the area. However, we also find a diverse social history, culture and complex grounded experiences at street level involving a wide range of residents and other users. These observations demonstrate how, even in the most elite of urban neighbourhoods, spaces remain socially complex and diverse, despite ongoing tensions.

papers.title: Virtual Flood Experience Enhances Preparedness Through Emotional and Neural Engagement
papers.authors: Fujimi, T., Kochiyama, T., Sato, W., Watanabe, M.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As climate change intensifies flood risks, strengthening individual preparedness is essential for sustainable societies. This study tested whether first‐person three‐dimensional computer graphics (3DCG) flood videos can complement official flood maps in motivating preparedness. We used these materials as operationalizations of experiential and descriptive information, respectively. In a preregistered web experiment with 1000 participants, those who viewed flood videos showed a small but statistically significant increase in preparedness intentions compared with those who viewed flood maps. Mediation analyses showed that, among the measured psychological variables, only fear had a significant indirect effect, suggesting that stimulus‐evoked fear helped explain this increase. We also conducted a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study with 45 participants using a within‐subjects design. Flood videos elicited greater right amygdala activation than flood maps, consistent with fear‐related processing. Together, these findings provide convergent behavioral and neural evidence that first‐person 3DCG flood videos evoke stronger fear‐related responses than flood maps and that subjective fear helps account for their effect on preparedness intentions. The results suggest that visually vivid flood videos may complement map‐based communication by increasing emotional salience and promoting flood‐preparedness intentions.

papers.title: Multi-hazard assessment of the eastern slope of the Sistema de Famatina, La Rioja province (Argentina)
papers.authors: María Cecilia Corbat, Oscar Juárez, Enrique Fucks, José Augusto Casas
papers.abstract: Abstract In the eastern sector of the Sistema de Famatina, both natural processes and anthropogenic activities pose considerable risks to the landscape and its inhabitants. This study investigates the geohazards and environmental agents that have historically affected the region, with a focus on their implications for local communities and territories. The analysis integrates case studies of documented natural events, identification of mitigation strategies, satellite imagery interpretation, landform recognition, and direct field observations. In addition, meteorological, hydrological, seismic, and demographic data were compiled to identify previously undocumented events with the potential to generate significant socio-environmental impacts. The study area is subject to a range of natural hazards, including those originated by meteorological events (e.g., intense precipitation and strong winds), fluvial processes (e.g., avulsion, gully erosion, and flooding), mass movement processes (e.g., landslides and rockfalls), and seismic activity. Our results reveal the recurrent nature of these hazards; in general, their consequences are compounded by anthropogenic pressures, including land-use changes, variations in land cover, and environmental pollution. Collectively, these factors intensify existing socio-environmental issues. This research contributes to sustainable environmental management by considering plausible future scenarios and hazard interactions. Our findings are intended to inform local and regional socio-economic development strategies and to serve as a scientific resource for policymakers and planners. Furthermore, by enhancing awareness of ongoing and recurring hazards, the study supports community resilience building and the reduction of adverse impacts at the local level.

papers.title: Likelihood-robust fusion of crowdsourced road-passability reports for flood relief dispatch and UAV inspection targeting
papers.authors: Hailong Li, Ya Li, Xiangnan Song
papers.abstract: Abstract Flood emergency agencies increasingly combine crowdsourced road reports with scarce unmanned-aerial-vehicle (UAV) inspections, yet panic, stale forwarding, and deliberate rumours can distort road-passability beliefs and redirect relief. This study develops a decision framework for fusing reports when source credibility is uncertain or adversarially exploited and for choosing whether the next trusted observation should inspect a road or recalibrate a reporting source. Credibility is represented by a data-driven ambiguity set and rumours by bounded contamination, yielding a distributionally robust credal posterior and min-max dispatch. We derive the dual value of verification-road-state clarification and calibration spillover-and prove a contamination threshold τ* at which the preferred action switches from road inspection to source recalibration. We further bound robust loss and characterize a strategic relocating attacker. On synthetic benchmarks, non-robust regret rises from 142 to 297 stranded passengers as contamination reaches 0.5, whereas robust regret remains within 105-168; the predicted switch occurs near τ* = 0.13-0.16. In a replay of the 20 July 2021 Zhengzhou flood, non-robust fusion reverses a blocked-road assessment and propagates error across about 62 cells, while robust fusion preserves the assessment and one verification recalibrates about 59 reports. In a Zhengzhou road-network decision test, eight baselines incur 233-300 stranded-passenger equivalents under the rumour, whereas the robust policy retains clean-evidence delivery. The framework provides flood-response agencies with a principled rule for allocating scarce verification when crowdsourced road information may be unreliable or manipulated.

papers.title: Early warning system for non-seismic gravity driven tsunamis
papers.authors: Giorgio Lacanna, M. Ripepe
papers.abstract: Gravity-driven mass flows represent a significant near-field hazard in volcanic environments and, increasingly, in coastal regions affected by climate-driven slope instability. Despite their destructive potential, quantitative assessments of real-time detection systems operating under natural conditions remain scarce. Here we present the performance and sensitivity of the tsunami early-warning system currently operating at Stromboli Volcano (Italy), based on offshore pressure gauges and a real-time detection algorithm. Sixteen years of sea-level records (2010–2026), including 63 tsunamis events ranging from 0.02 to 2 m height, show that the system issues alert within less than 22 s from the tsunami onset and tens of seconds before its maximum amplitude, with no false alarms. A sensitivity analysis, based on Peak-Over-Threshold statistics and extreme wave modeling, demonstrates that the detection capability remains effective even under extreme sea state conditions also for tsunami with height as low as 4 m. To support regional tsunami warning and reduce the alerts for tsunami with no inundation effects on a distant (> 10 km) coasts, we apply real-time Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD), which successfully extracts tsunami signals and preserves waveform characteristics. EEMD also isolates longer period sea level oscillations associated with atmospheric pressure waves within the meteotsunami frequency band, demonstrating the applicability of the method to multiple classes of non-seismic tsunamis. This work provides the first long-term quantitative evaluation of an operational near-field early-warning system for volcanogenic tsunamis and proposes a transferable multi-tier framework for landslide-tsunami and meteotsunami hazard mitigation for coastal environments worldwide.

papers.title: Smartphone mobility data reveals how home-location heat and park cooling shape park visitation in Los Angeles
papers.authors: Yongli Tang, Xiang Li, Xiao Huang et al.
papers.abstract: Parks can support climate adaptation by providing cooling, but their use is shaped by residents’ cooling needs, parks’ cooling potential and the ability to reach them. Little is known about how residential heat exposure and relative park cooling, measured by the home-park temperature difference, jointly relate to park visitation from an origin-destination perspective. Using mobile phone data and explainable Random Forest models, we examine these associations across park types and demographic groups in Los Angeles County. Results show that local-park visitation was generally negatively associated with home-location temperature, whereas visitation to regional parks and natural areas increased above approximately 35 °C. However, greater visitation did not necessarily correspond to trips to cooler parks relative to home locations. For local parks, greater relative cooling was associated with higher visitation, and this association strengthened as home-location temperature increased. Under extreme heat, the positive cooling-visitation association was strongest in predominantly Hispanic, Asian, and low-income communities. In contrast, visitation to regional parks and natural areas generally peaked when park and home temperatures were similar, with greater cooling not associated with higher visitation. Spatial accessibility may partly explain these differences. Home-park distance was the leading predictor across all park types. Greater cooling at regional parks and natural areas was often associated with longer travel distances and lower transit availability, potentially limiting access to these cooling opportunities. These findings highlight the need to improve cooling capacity in local parks serving socially vulnerable populations while reducing access barriers to larger green spaces during extreme heat.

papers.title: Impact of global supply chain pressures on energy demand and stability: The role of global sustainability initiatives
papers.authors: Riazullah Shinwari, Junyi Feng, Nazim Hussain, Shah Mir Mowahed
papers.abstract: Global supply chain pressures (GSCP) have become a major challenge for multinational enterprises (MNEs), influencing firm-level operational decisions, including evolving energy demand patterns. This paper investigates the impact of global supply chain pressures on energy consumption in Chinese MNEs from 2013 to 2022. Results from Double-Selection Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) linear regression indicate that GSCP increases the energy demand of Chinese MNEs. One possible explanation is that GSCP undermines production stability and operational efficiency, prompting firms to intensify production, extend operating hours, and adopt additional shifts to meet volatile demand conditions. Furthermore, global shocks (i.e., US-China Trade War and COVID-19) and global green initiatives (i.e., Montreal Protocol–Kigali Amendment, the EU Innovation Fund, and the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative) significantly moderate the relationship between GSCP and energy demand. The heterogeneity analysis exhibits that the GSCP impact is most pronounced among state-owned MNEs, firms with substantial overseas investment experience, and enterprises exhibiting lower degrees of internationalisation. This study contributes new empirical and theoretical insights into how global supply chain disruptions affect corporate energy demand and shape the strategic responses of Chinese MNEs.

papers.title: Towards high-resolution forecasting of tropical deforestation with deep learning
papers.authors: Jan Pišl, Gencer Sümbül, Gaston Lenczner et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Reducing tropical deforestation effectively requires spatially explicit data on deforestation dynamics. While past deforestation is now detected and mapped with high accuracy, producing reliable future forecasts remains a challenge. We present a deep learning approach for high-resolution deforestation forecasting in the Brazilian Amazon. We train a spatio-temporal ConvLSTM model on past deforestation maps and other covariates. Our model achieves an F1 score of 0.47 when forecasting one year ahead, substantially improving over comparable prior work. For multi-year predictions, we obtain promising results within a 3-year horizon, while sensitivity to shifts in deforestation dynamics suggests limitations for longer-term forecasts. We generate forecasts for years 2016–2018 across the Brazilian Amazon, and make them available through an interactive Google Earth Engine application. Our results demonstrate the potential for high-resolution, short- and medium-term forecasting that can support conservation efforts and help protect tropical forests.

papers.title: Post-harvest stages account for more than half of seafood carbon footprint
papers.authors: Yuanchao Hu, Weiwei Lu, 张浩冉 et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Seafood is increasingly important for healthy dietary transitions in modern urban lifestyles. Yet, the patterns of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions remain poorly understood, which hinders the low-carbon pathways for city-specific seafood supply chains. Here, we constructed a disaggregated supply chain dataset to quantify the GHG footprint of consumption of five major seafood categories across 313 Chinese cities. In 2023, total GHG footprint of Chinese seafood consumption reached 182.6 Mt CO₂-eq (1.5% of the national total emissions), dominated by shellfish (65.7%) and fish (25.1%). Annual per-capita emissions varied from over 1000 kg CO₂-eq/capita in coastal and tourism cities to near zero in many inland cities. Spatially, 79.9% of emissions were concentrated in coastal cities, with the top five cities contributing 27.2%. Most transported seafood (58–88%) was within 200 km, indicating shorter food miles than other food categories. We find that off-farm supply chain stages, which account for 55% of total emissions, are key to retaining seafood's low-carbon advantage over terrestrial protein sources such as chicken and pork. We highlight the need for coordinated strategies to support both sustainable and healthy diets, including efficient mariculture practices in coastal cities and low-carbon cold-chain logistics and feed production in the supply chain.

papers.title: Adapting with justice: a governance framework for equitable urban resilience beyond the environmental justice triad
papers.authors: Sarker, M., Ning, Z., Feng, W., Al Mamun, M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Urban adaptation can redistribute protection, public investment, land value, and displacement risk across neighborhoods and social groups. This scoping review, reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, synthesized scholarship on justice, governance, and equitable urban resilience. Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language publications from January 2000 through February 2026, supplemented by backward reference checking. After duplicate removal, title/abstract screening, and full-text assessment, 79 studies were included. A combined deductive–inductive thematic synthesis, organized with MAXQDA Analytics Pro, identified three interlocking governance pillars: justice architectures, accountable co-production, and context-tuned strategies. Across the included studies, equitable adaptation was repeatedly discussed in relation to enforceable rights, distributional targeting, meaningful community authority, attention to compound and context-specific risks, anti-displacement safeguards, and durable operations and maintenance. By contrast, consultation without decision authority and adaptation investment without housing protection were described as risks for reproducing exclusion, unequal access, and climate gentrification. The review translates these patterns into five assessable governance checkpoints: rights and intergenerational accountability, distributional targeting, shared decision authority, scale and compound-risk fit, and anti-displacement protection and benefit durability. The resulting framework is an analytically derived and testable governance framework rather than a validated causal model. It provides a structured basis for evaluating whether urban adaptation is environmentally effective, socially just, institutionally accountable, and durable over time.

papers.title: Anthropogenic climate change intensifies rainfall in extreme compound rainfall-wave events in the NW Mediterranean
papers.authors: Aguilera-Vidal, M., Wahl, T., Jiménez, J.
papers.abstract: Abstract The concurrent occurrence of extreme rainfall and energetic wave conditions can generate compound coastal hazards with impacts exceeding those produced by either driver alone. Although recent studies have identified changes in rainfall-wave extremes along the northwestern Mediterranean coast, whether these changes can be attributed to anthropogenic climate remains unclear. Here, we investigate the anthropogenic influence on compound rainfall-wave extremes using five initial-condition ensemble members of the CMIP6 MRI-ESM2.0 model from the Detection and Attribution Model Intercomparison Project, comparing factual (ALL) and counterfactual (NAT) experiments over 1961–2020. Changes in dependence and joint return periods are assessed using Kendall’s τ-b and copula-based analyses. No robust anthropogenic signal is detected in the observed strengthening of rainfall-wave dependence, as neither its temporal evolution nor the change in dependence structure identified in ERA5 is consistently reproduced across the ensemble. In contrast, the ALL-NAT comparison suggests an anthropogenic contribution to rainfall intensification in the most extreme compound events, while wave changes remain small and variable across realizations. For example, fitted estimates associate a rainfall-wave combination of P24h ≈320 mm and Hs ≈4 m with joint return periods of approximately 50 years under NAT and 25 years under ALL. This comparison is indicative, with its magnitude subject to uncertainties in event sampling, marginal fitting, and copula estimation that have yet to be quantified. Agreement with ERA5 supports the model’s representation of baseline characteristics, although further evaluation would strengthen confidence in its response to external forcing. Overall, the findings suggest rainfall intensification within the model framework, while the associated frequency change should be interpreted with caution.

papers.title: Satellite observations and energy balance constrain the thermal footprint of a hyperscale data-centre cluster
papers.authors: Jing, J.
papers.abstract: Abstract Whether hyperscale data centres (DCs) warm their surroundings divides current evidence: a coarse-resolution satellite preprint attributes ∼2 °C of land-surface-temperature (LST) warming to facilities worldwide (Marinoni et al 2026 arXiv: 2603.20897v3 ), while peer-reviewed transects near Phoenix measure +0.7–0.9 °C of near-ground air warming a few hundred metres downwind (Sailor et al 2026 J. Eng. Sustain. Bldgs. Cities 7 024501). Prospective anthropogenic-heat models remain untested against long-term observations, and no major DC market assesses local temperature impact before construction. We provide the first ex-post, controlled satellite test for Japan’s largest DC concentration, the Inzai and Tama clusters near Tokyo, whose staggered build-out (twelve facilities, 2011–2025) yields a three-phase event study with replication. The test combines daytime Landsat (2013–2026), 70 m day/night ECOSTRESS and 1 km MODIS with matched pre-2013 controls, facility-level energy disclosures and minimum-detectable-effect analysis, gated by an air-temperature energy-balance ceiling (∼0.35 °C, cluster scale, night) that bounds LST a fortiori . Commissioning cools the daytime LST by 1.8 °C–2.2 °C—significant under all three reference types, a radiative-property signal opposite in sign to the viral claim. Deep-night facility-scale LST changes are indistinguishable from zero (bounded below ∼0.6 °C–1.2 °C), and the cluster-scale night LST bound (0.24 °C–0.29 °C, autocorrelation-corrected, two platforms) closes beneath the air-temperature ceiling. The exclusion of warming at the claimed magnitude rests primarily on energy balance—+ 2 °C, even in air, would require 6–43 times the available waste heat—with observations supplying consistent bounds at every scale they resolve. Arid- and continental-climate consistency checks (Phoenix and DeKalb) reproduce the decomposition: in both, night surface warming is largely in place during construction—before any server load—and matches neighbouring non-DC development; conversion, not exhaust. Near-source air warming is real where rejection density is high and climates dry; kilometre-scale surface warming from waste heat is unattainable. The protocol is the ex-post verification tool siting regimes lack.

papers.title: Evaluating mangrove establishment trajectories and carbon recovery potential using a spatial age-based framework
papers.authors: Zhao, Y., Li, T., Zheng, B., Wang, X. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Mangrove restoration is a vital nature-based solution for climate change mitigation and biodiversity conservation. However, large-scale mangrove restoration success is predominantly evaluated using area-based metrics, which fail to capture the complex temporal trajectories of forest structural and functional recovery. Stand age directly determines structural heterogeneity and carbon stocks, making it a key indicator for monitoring recovery trajectories and estimating carbon stocks. We developed a spatial age-based framework to map established mangrove stands and quantify the existing carbon stock and remaining potential. To this end, we combined an optimized LandTrendr change-detection algorithm with age-stratified logistic growth models using Landsat time-series data. We generated a 30-m resolution age map of all established mangroves from 2000 to 2023 across tropical Hainan Island, China. Our results identified 337 ha of established mangroves as of 2023. Notably, >50% (173 ha) of the detected stands are ⩽7 years old yet have already attained 43% of mature forest carbon stocks, whereas only 4% of them have reached ⩾15 years. Under continued protection, these forests are expected to store an estimated 33 668 Mg C (27 971–38 902 Mg C), with the greatest potential concentrated in the Dongzhaigang area. Conversely, the limited extent of older forests (4% of the established area) already secures significant recovered carbon stocks, warranting urgent protection. This contrast underscores the necessity of differentiated management strategies calibrated to both restoration scale and stand development stage. Ultimately, this spatially explicit framework informs evidence-based management to improve restoration outcomes and provides actionable baselines for national carbon credit markets.

papers.title: Impact of different on-road vehicle emissions inventories on downstream air quality, exposure, health, and equity assessments
papers.authors: Shlipak, K., Lang, V., Santiago, M., Tessum, C. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Emissions from on-road vehicles are a pervasive source of air pollution, contributing to inequitable pollutant exposure and adverse health outcomes. Numerical air quality models are used to characterize traffic-related pollutant concentrations and impacts. However, model outputs rely on underlying emissions inventories whose formulations can differ substantially. Here, we leverage the widely used Intervention Model for Air Pollution (InMAP) to examine how four different on-road emissions inventories used at three different spatial resolutions (1, 1.3, and 4 km) influence simulated fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) population exposure, health impacts, and equity outcomes in a freight-heavy urban setting—the Greater Chicago Region. We find that population-weighted exposure and attributable mortality differ up to 72% and 69% across inventories, compared to only 14%–17% across resolutions. While all inventories result in higher estimated PM 2.5 exposure and mortality among Black, Hispanic, and Asian populations compared to non-Hispanic White populations, the magnitude and relative ordering of disparities across racial groups vary with both inventory choice and spatial resolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that characterizing exposure inequities using emissions colocation can yield substantially different disparity estimates (up to 20%) from pollutant concentration-based estimates due to atmospheric transport and chemistry— a divergence that likely represents a lower bound given InMAP’s reduced-complexity parameterizations. This work builds on recent studies showing that model resolution influences air quality, health, and equity assessments by demonstrating that on-road emissions inventory choice introduces even greater differences than spatial resolution.

papers.title: Modeling freshwater use for direct lithium extraction from geothermal brines in the Salton Sea
papers.authors: Gunawardhana, L., Busse, M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Global lithium demand is projected to more than double by 2035, to about 715 kt per year (3.8 Mt lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) per year) under the International Energy Agency Stated Policies Scenario, intensifying the need for new, sustainable extraction routes. Direct lithium extraction (DLE) from geothermal brines is of particular interest because co-location with closed-loop geothermal operations avoids the large land footprint of evaporation ponds and the carbon intensity of hard-rock mining. The Salton Sea Known Geothermal Resource Area (SS-KGRA) hosts geothermal plants with co-located pilot-scale DLE facilities and is one of the most advanced regions for geothermal lithium extraction. Though these operations are expected to reduce land and carbon intensity, they require freshwater inputs across multiple unit operations; this demand has been reported only as facility-wide aggregates, without process-level resolution, even though the SS-KGRA lies in an arid region where water supply is largely committed to agriculture. Existing estimates do not track the internal fate of process water, which determines the net volume drawn from external sources. Herein, we present LiHydroSim, a process-based model that translates publicly available process descriptions into a facility-level freshwater balance through a three-layer architecture separating gross unit-operation demand, internal recovery, and net external supply. Applied to a representative adsorption-based facility processing 7000 gallons per minute of geothermal brine, the model estimates net external freshwater demand of 1719 acre-feet per year (152 m 3 t − 1 LCE; 0.12 AF/t LCE), below the 189–355 m 3 t − 1 LCE (0.15–0.29 AF/t LCE) reported by Salton Sea developers, consistent with auxiliary demands outside the process boundary. The eluant for lithium elution dominates the water balance, accounting for 92% of gross internal process-water demand, while internal recycling offsets roughly one third of that gross demand. Total demand depends mainly on eluant volume: across two patent-specified operating modes, it ranges from 870 to 1719 acre-feet per year.

papers.title: Deep learning reveals severe shelterbelt degradation in eastern Ukraine due to the war
papers.authors: Myroniuk, V., Khan, Y., Sovakov, O., Matsala, M. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has caused extensive damage to forests, particularly in eastern and southern regions with sustained combat, where field shelterbelts have often been used as cover and subsequently heavily destroyed. This study presents a systematic region-scale assessment of pre-war shelterbelt area and war-related loss between 2021 and 2025 using 3 m PlanetScope imagery and deep learning. We evaluated three input datasets—monthly PlanetScope RGB mosaics, multiseasonal PlanetScope RGB stacks, and surface reflectance (SR) PlanetScope imagery—in combination with two semantic segmentation architectures: a convolutional U-Net with a ResNet-34 encoder and a transformer-based SegFormer with a MiT-B0 backbone. Across all input configurations, the U-Net consistently outperformed SegFormer, achieving the highest F 1 scores. Monthly RGB mosaics delivered accuracy comparable to more complex multiseasonal and SR inputs in pixel-based evaluation and are a cost-efficient option for mapping narrow shelterbelts. The RGB-based model trained on July 2021 mosaics reached an F 1 score of 0.71 and retained values of 0.58–0.67 for other months of the same leaf-on season. Temporal transfer to 2025 resulted in lower but still reasonable performance with F 1 scores of 0.53–0.63. Error-adjusted mapping estimated the shelterbelt area in 2021 at 254 ± 14.5 thousand ha, equivalent to a mean density of 2.6 ha km −2 . By 2025, this area had been reduced by approximately 41 thousand ha, or 16% of the pre-war area. Losses were strongly concentrated along frontlines where local losses exceeded 1.5 ha km −2 compared to an average loss of 0.5 ha km −2 across the entire study area. The resulting maps complement the existing forest monitoring framework in Ukraine and provide a spatially explicit basis for prioritizing post-war remediation and assessing losses in protective functions and carbon accumulation.

papers.title: To VR or not to VR? Lessons learnt and future pathways for developing Virtual Reality in experimental urban research
papers.authors: Tuuli Toivonen, Elias S. Willberg, Reza Aghanejad et al.
papers.abstract: The use of Virtual Reality (VR) in experimental urban studies is increasing rapidly. Scholars from a broad range of disciplines, such as geography, environmental psychology, urban planning, and health research, are increasingly using VR for studying peoples' preferences and behaviour in varying urban conditions. While VR provides novel possibilities for experimental research, setting up a VR environment is resource-intensive and requires careful planning across multiple phases, including project inception, environment creation, testing, empirical implementation, and packaging for later use. In this paper, we focus on aspects often left out from empirical research articles: the technical and practical decisions needed to establish a VR environment for experimental research. We synthesize lessons learnt from 13 European projects that have employed VR to investigate human preferences and behaviour in varying urban conditions. The experiences were collected from involved researchers through a survey, and the lessons and recommendations where further refined in a joint workshop. Based on this collective experience and knowledge, we discuss critical technical and administrative aspects in VR development and implementation, such as the choice between in-house versus outsourced development, the integration of realistic environmental features, minimizing cybersickness among participants, and ensuring the longevity of the project. We present a framework for VR development as part of empirical urban studies and offer concrete recommendations, with the aim to lower barriers for using VR in experimental research. We conclude by providing directions for a more scalable, collaborative, and inclusive future for VR in urban research.

papers.title: WBGT assessment in transitional urban spaces using a radiation-resolved framework extended from indoor to outdoor conditions
papers.authors: Behrooz Khalili Nasr, Shayan Mirzabeigi, Alireza Khodayarkhani, Andrea Giovanni Mainini
papers.abstract: Outdoor heat stress assessment in transitional urban spaces depends on spatially varying shortwave and longwave radiation, particularly under partial shading. This study extends a framework linking radiation inputs to WBGT, previously developed for indoor solar exposure, to an outdoor transitional corridor between two buildings in Milan. Hourly shortwave irradiance incident on a discretized human manikin was calculated using a geometry-resolved model accounting for direct, diffuse, transmitted, and reflected components. Time-varying exterior surface temperatures from a building energy simulation determined longwave mean radiant temperature. The shortwave and longwave components were combined through a shortwave adjustment and propagated through a tailored WBGT calculation against activity-dependent reference limits. Sensitivity was evaluated across six canopy configurations, six air speeds, three ground surfaces, and dry-bulb temperature increments of +2, +4, and +6°C. At the central position and 0.5 m/s, the share of working-hour records with no limit exceeded rose from 69.9% (no canopy) to 92.0% (opaque canopy), while the share with all limits exceeded fell from 8.4% to zero. Increasing air speed reduced WBGT exceedance most under the no-canopy condition, with a smaller effect beneath the opaque canopy. Ground-surface differences were concentrated under exposed conditions. A 90%-transmittance canopy changed exceedance little because longwave emission offset reduced shortwave exposure. Prescribed warming shifted WBGT distributions upward, while the 50%-transmittance canopy lowered exceedance at every warming level. The framework provides a common radiation-resolved screening basis linking this outdoor assessment to the previous indoor framework, without implying equivalent subjective comfort in both environments pending field validation.

papers.title: Classifying type-specific green space using satellite imagery and LiDAR to assess associations with diabetes prevalence
papers.authors: Scarlett B. Rakowska, Haoxuan Ge, Matthew Adams
papers.abstract: Abstract Urban green space is often measured by using greenness indices, such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index, but these indices do not distinguish among green space types. This study integrated 3-metre spatial resolution multispectral imagery and LiDAR-derived normalized Digital Surface Models (nDSM) to classify type-specific green spaces across Mississauga, Ontario, and examine their associations with diabetes prevalence. We tested eight combinations of spectral bands, vegetation and water indices, and structural data using an object-based random forest and found that the best-performing model included all the bands, indices, and nDSM, achieving 88% overall classification accuracy. The classification identified deciduous trees, coniferous trees, shrubs, grass, and marsh/wetland, which were then linked to census tract-level diabetes prevalence using local and neighbourhood beta regression models by sex and age group, and adjusted for socioeconomic covariates. Deciduous trees, coniferous trees, and shrubs were more consistently associated with lower diabetes prevalence, particularly among adults aged 45 years and older. NDVI-based models showed weaker associations with diabetes prevalence after adjustment, while type-specific models retained associations. These findings suggest that type-specific green space and structure provide more informative measures of exposure than greenness alone. Integrating high spatial resolution multispectral imagery and LiDAR provides a methodological framework for health research examining relationships between urban green space and chronic diseases.

papers.title: The Aftermath of Almost: Communicating Risk Amid Community Narratives of Near Misses
papers.authors: Ray, E., Schramm, A., Merle, P.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Unpredictable weather means that serious threats do not always unfold as forecast. Hurricane near misses create an especially challenging communication context: The absence of harm may invite community explanations that make the event feel less threatening, even as future risk persists. This study examines how community narratives and post‐event risk messages shape risk perception, collective efficacy, preparedness intentions, message sharing, and credibility after hurricane near misses. In an online experiment, Florida residents ( N = 405) viewed social media posts about a hurricane that shifted away from a coastal community. The posts varied by explanation type, comparing a symbolic community narrative with a factual account, and by response source, comparing emergency management, peer, and control messages. Results show limits and leverage points for post‐event risk communication: In the primary analysis, neither community narratives nor risk messages significantly shifted perceived risk; however, supplementary analyses accounting for regional residence revealed a small reduction in perceived risk following narrative exposure. Risk messages increased sharing and collective efficacy, and organizational sources were more credible than peer sources. These findings suggest that post‐event risk communication after near misses may not readily recalibrate individual risk perceptions but can shape how risk information circulates and how communities perceive their capacity to respond. The study advances understanding of near misses as ambiguous risk events in which communication matters even when harm does not occur.

papers.title: Identification and Governance Strategy of Urban Systemic Risk Induced by Extreme Rain–Snow–Ice Weather in Southern China
papers.authors: Feng, W., Zhang, G.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT China's rapid urbanization has expanded urban spatial scale and increased the concentration of population, wealth, and infrastructure. Against the background of climate change, urban systemic risk induced by extreme rain–snow–ice weather (USR–RSI) in southern China has repeatedly disrupted critical infrastructure and public services, generating cascading impacts across interconnected urban systems. This study examines the generation and evolution of USR–RSI and develops a corresponding resilience governance strategy. Building on conceptual analysis, complex network theory and system vulnerability theory are integrated to construct the theoretical framework. A causal loop diagram is used to characterize risk diffusion and feedback mechanisms based on the 2008 and 2024 RSI disaster cases. Semi‐structured interviews and documentary materials are further analyzed using a structured data analysis approach to identify sensitivity and adaptive factors associated with node and path vulnerability. On the basis of these findings, a whole‐process resilience governance framework is proposed, covering resilience construction, integration of warning and response, rapid recovery, and long‐term adaptive optimization and transformative reconfiguration. The study provides an empirical and analytical basis for understanding and governing USR–RSI from the perspective of interconnected urban socio‐technical systems.

papers.title: Risk‐Oriented Differentiated Governance for Ambiguous Information
papers.authors: Ni, P., Zhu, J., Zhang, H.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence has led to an exponential increase in false information, especially ambiguous information. Hampered by resource constraints, conventional governance approaches fall short of enabling efficient and precise risk management. In response, this paper innovatively proposes a risk‐oriented tiered governance framework tailored to ambiguous information. Specifically, we quantify epistemic uncertainty via multi‐level semantic features, combine it with network propagation features to determine latent influence scores, and construct a risk function capturing their synergy. Critical and acceptable boundaries are introduced to categorize ambiguous information into discrete risk levels, tier‐specific governance strategies are devised, and a propagation throttling (limiting each user's successful forwards per ambiguous information) strategy is innovatively proposed for medium‐risk information. Finally, we simulate differentiated governance strategies across risk levels of ambiguous information, systematically assess governance effectiveness, and offer a comparative discussion grounded in fairness and ethics. This study offers an operational analytical framework for refined risk governance of ambiguous information, contributes methodological innovations in risk quantification modeling and tiered governance strategies, and provides theoretical support and practical guidance for risk management authorities in designing differentiated measures.

papers.title: Hybrid Semi‐Quantitative Risk Assessment for Aging Offshore Platforms: A HAZOP–FMEA–Bow‐Tie Framework With Sensitivity Analysis and KRI‐Based Governance
papers.authors: Saleem, M., Baseer, M., Tariq, Q., Khan, A.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Aging offshore installations increasingly operate beyond their original design life, yet conventional periodic risk assessments capture barrier degradation only intermittently. This study presents a barrier‐conditioned semi‐quantitative risk‐assessment workflow that integrates Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), and bow‐tie barrier analysis. The workflow combines decomposed residual likelihood and consequence scoring with threshold‐stability testing and a Key Risk Indicator (KRI)‐based update rule. Its principal contribution is the governance linkage: an explicit rule set that maps barrier condition and KRI threshold breaches to changes in residual likelihood, residual consequence, and risk band between formal safety‐case reviews. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the workflow is demonstrated through a fully synthetic scenario representing a life‐extended semi‐submersible installation; all inputs are constructed and explicitly identified throughout as scenario assumptions. Under the illustrative scoring assumptions, a 19‐hazard register spanning seven hazard categories yields two high, nine medium, and eight low residual risks, with blowout/well‐control failure and hydrogen sulfide release remaining the highest residual risks. Per‐perturbation threshold‐stability analysis and distribution‐based Monte Carlo propagation indicate that 16 of the 19 residual risk ratings are sensitive to classification boundaries, suggesting that the reported scores should be interpreted as central estimates subject to uncertainty. The proposed workflow provides a transparent tool for risk screening and governance support, complementing full quantitative risk assessment (QRA) while preserving its essential analytical role.

papers.title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
papers.authors: Laura Gibbs, CHRIS D. JONES, ﻿Colin Jones et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract When anthropogenic CO 2 emissions cease, global temperature does not stabilize immediately. The resulting global temperature change, the zero emissions commitment, is central to carbon budget assessments and understanding reversibility of global warming, yet its dependence on prior warming levels remains unclear. Here we show, using zero-emission simulations with the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.2) across global warming levels of 1.5–5 K, that the zero emissions commitment stays near zero up to 2 K but becomes positive at higher warming levels, reaching 0.4–0.6 K after ~ 150 years. This dependence indicates that stabilizing or reversing warming becomes progressively more difficult as peak temperature rises. We identify the mechanism behind this behaviour: stronger warming from higher radiative disequilibrium and weakening carbon sinks, driven by saturated land carbon uptake and the reduced radiative impact of CO 2 drawdown at higher background CO 2 concentrations. Higher peak warming therefore commits the planet to additional warming, limiting temperature-overshoot reversibility.

papers.title: Hurricane disturbance leads to elevated wildfire activity in the Gulf Coast region U.S.A.
papers.authors: Harper Steele, Richard S. Vachula, Peter C. Ryan
papers.abstract: Abstract Building on long-standing hypotheses of a hurricane-fire interaction, this study assesses empirical evidence for hurricane-driven increases in wildfire activity along the Gulf Coast of the United States. It has been proposed that wildfire risk is elevated post-hurricane due to increased fuel accumulation and alterations to forest microclimates associated with treefall (e.g., increased radiation, temperature, aridity). While isolated studies have identified evidence supporting this relationship using premodern proxy data, an analysis using modern empirical data is lacking. This study addresses this gap by using spatial analysis of contemporary hurricane and wildfire data to evaluate changes in wildfire activity following hurricane landfall events. Thirty hurricanes that made landfall between 1992 and 2019 (Category 1 to 5) were analyzed alongside wildfire data surrounding their path of destruction from the five years before and after each storm. In the five years after hurricanes, increases were seen in both the number of wildfires and total area burned, though spatial and temporal variation are apparent along the coastline. Of the three subregions studied, the Florida Peninsula experienced the largest increase in wildfire activity, primarily in the two and three years following hurricanes. Wildfire activity following select hurricanes is compared to fire weather index data to ensure observed trends are attributable to hurricane damage rather than background climatic factors. These results support the hypothesis of a hurricane-fire interaction and demonstrate that hurricanes continue to influence Gulf Coast fire regimes in the modern era, despite widespread fire suppression and prescribed burning efforts.

papers.title: Transferable machine learning prediction of urban pluvial flood water depth using multi-resolution digital elevation models
papers.authors: Babak Razdar, Ilenia Manco, Pasquale Giovanni Schiano et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Machine learning methods, particularly Random Forest (RF), present an effective solution for predicting urban pluvial flood water depth, especially in data-scarce regions where traditional hydrological and hydraulic observations are lacking. This study proposes a DEM-centric RF framework for predicting spatially continuous urban flood water depth across various precipitation return periods, emphasizing its robustness to terrain resolution degradation and spatial transferability. The model is trained and validated in Milan using a 1 m LiDAR-derived DEM and evaluated with a coarser 5 m EU-DEM to assess sensitivity to reduced resolution. Transferability is tested by applying the trained model to Cologne using independent 1 m LiDAR data. Model performance is assessed across five precipitation scenarios (5–100-year return periods) using absolute error metrics, tolerance thresholds, spatial diagnostics, and confidence-stratified analyses. Results show stable performance, with mean absolute errors below 0.30 m and over 58% of grid cells within ± 0.25 m of reference flood depths. Prediction errors are mainly found in hydraulically complex areas, while the majority of the urban domain shows well-constrained predictions. Confidence diagnostics indicate that high- and very-high-confidence predictions comply with tolerance thresholds under both DEM resolution degradation and spatial transfer. These findings suggest that relative terrain structure governs urban pluvial flooding patterns, enabling reliable flood depth predictions with medium-resolution DEMs. This framework offers a scalable tool for urban flood screening, hazard assessment, and climate adaptation planning in areas with limited data.

papers.title: Synoptic analysis and WRF sensitivity experiments of SACZ-driven extreme rainfall over Petropolis, Brazil
papers.authors: Miguel Amoedo, Fabrício Polifke da Silva
papers.abstract: Abstract Extreme rainfall in the mountainous region of Petrópolis (Brazil) is frequently associated with South Atlantic Convergence Zone (SACZ) episodes, low-level moisture, and complex terrain. Despite its operational relevance, the sensitivity of numerical forecasts to physical parameterizations under these high-impact environments remains poorly understood. This study evaluates the performance of the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model for five SACZ-driven extreme rainfall events using a 27–9–3 km nested configuration and an ensemble of 64 combinations of microphysics and cumulus schemes. A two-stage verification approach was applied, combining spatial qualitative assessment and quantitative metrics based on mean error, hourly root mean squared error (RMSE), temporal correlation, covariance, and POD–FAR diagnostics. The configurations highlighted in the spatial and temporal rainfall comparisons combined Ferrier microphysics (M5) with Tiedtke (C6) for 01–02 January 2012 and with New Simplified Arakawa–Schubert (C14) for 17–18 March 2013; WRF single-moment 5-class microphysics (M4) with New Tiedtke (C16) was highlighted for 08 March 2014. The 3-km grid generally preserves the shape of cumulative rainfall, but the mean daily bias changes from − 18 mm at 27 km to + 8 mm at 9 km and + 13 mm at 3 km. The present comparisons do not isolate the physical source of the 3-km bias. The findings demonstrate that the evaluated configurations and grid spacing both affect precipitation estimates for these five SACZ-related events. This study highlights key sources of uncertainty in operational forecasting over southeastern Brazil and provides guidance for optimizing physics configurations in similar mountainous, moisture-rich environments.
