papers.title: Evaluating urban street views through collective emotional perception from multimodal social media cityscape posts: An R-ECoT-based interpretable framework
papers.authors: Jianyu Fu, Xukang Wang, Jue Ma et al.
papers.abstract: Urban street views shape everyday urban experience, yet their assessment still relies largely on researcher-defined indicators and structured elicitation, with limited use of naturally occurring public responses. This study develops an interpretable framework that transforms social-media image–comment interactions into eight-dimensional collective emotional appraisals of urban scenes. Under approved access, 1078 Facebook and Instagram cityscape posts and 20,546 comments were retrieved through the SOMAR Virtual Data Enclave. Comment-derived Plutchik labels were assessed through human validation and robustness tests, then used as weak supervision for R-ECoT, which jointly predicts emotion intensities and generates emotion-specific grounding maps from images. The trained CLIP-based model was applied to 610,017 ZENRIN street-view images in Setagaya Ward, Tokyo, and predictions were aggregated to 10 m road segments. Comment-derived labels agreed more closely with an independent post-level human reference than the strongest image-only estimate (Pearson 0.818 versus 0.751). CLIP-R-ECoT achieved the best performance in hierarchical benchmarks, with a KL divergence of 0.329, an MSE of 0.0106, and a balanced accuracy of 0.757. Its grounding maps showed greater random-corrected masking faithfulness than Grad-CAM (0.083 versus 0.049), higher perturbation stability, and lower spatial fragmentation. Street-level mapping revealed differentiated emotional patterns, while emotion-specific high-response regions in the images were associated with distinct semantic, color-atmospheric, and depth-structural attributes. By converting dispersed public reactions into spatially continuous and interpretable evidence, the framework supports fine-grained streetscape screening, helps identify locations warranting closer inspection, and directs design attention toward the visible conditions associated with different public responses.

papers.title: Forest landscapes determine their pests: jack pine budworm spatial dynamics under host scarcity
papers.authors: Barry J. Cooke, Brian R. Sturtevant, Dan Kneeshaw et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Context Jack pine budworm (JPBW), Choristoneura pinus pinus, is a major defoliator in Canada, yet remains absent from theoretical discourse on outbreak synchrony, despite sharing key life history traits with the archetypal “cross-scale” pest, spruce budworm (C. fumiferana). JPBW has primarily been studied in host-rich landscapes, raising questions about its behavior in host-sparse regions. Objectives We asked whether scale-crossing JPBW outbreaks are contingent on host density, and whether reduced outbreak incidence in host-sparse landscapes reflects synchronized or desynchronized population limitation. Methods We applied a systematic framework for analyzing spatiotemporal tree-ring data, adapted from recent reconstructions of spruce budworm and forest tent caterpillar. This framework integrates temporal and spatial methods to evaluate periodicity, coherence, and landscape-scale synchrony. Results In the pine-sparse Border Lakes region (~30,000 km 2 ), we identified 14 growth disturbances between 1910 and 2006, typically recurring every seven years and affecting 30% of trees annually at peak. Reanalysis of data from a host-rich site in Manitoba confirmed strong correspondence between JPBW defoliation and growth reductions. Nine episodes in the host-rich site coincided with published outbreaks, whereas signals in the host-sparse Border Lakes remained spatially variable and weakly correlated across sample areas. Conclusions Despite high fecundity and dispersal potential, JPBW in host-sparse landscapes behaves endemically. Pest status, we argue, is not a fixed insect trait but an emergent property of host availability and spatial scale. The JPBW system constitutes a third example from the Border Lakes region where the “catastrophe” theory of outbreak origin is more consistent with data than a “clockwork” theory of spatially synchronized cycling.

papers.title: Non-land-use forcing significantly drives projected trends of atmospheric black carbon over Africa: Implications for mitigation strategies
papers.authors: Matthews Nyasulu, Genesis Magara, Fabiano Gibson Daud Thulu et al.
papers.abstract: Black carbon (BC) plays a critical role in climate forcing and poses significant health risks, yet its trends and drivers remain poorly constrained across Africa. Here, we quantify the relative contributions of land-use and non-land-use forcing to the projected trends of BC using the Meteorological Research Institute Earth System Model version 2.0 (MRI-ESM2-0) under the Aerosol Chemistry Model Intercomparison Project (AerChemMIP). A variance decomposition framework is applied to SSP370SST and SSP370SST-SSP126Lu simulations to isolate land-use from non-land-use forcing. The MRI-ESM2-0 model reproduces spatial patterns well (r > 0.8, p < 0.05), although spatially heterogeneous biases persist over Central Africa. Elevated BC concentration (>0.7 μg m −3 ) occurs in Central and West Africa, while low (<0.1) concentrations occur in parts of North Africa and the island of Madagascar. Projected trends reveal a statistically significant increase in BC (p < 0.05) over North and West Africa, whereas Central and Southern Africa show decreasing trends in BC until 2100. The projected trends are primarily driven by non-land-use emissions, with the influence of hydroclimatic changes, while land-use forcing is most pronounced in Central and Southern Africa. These findings highlight the need for region-specific mitigation strategies to control future BC concentrations across Africa effectively.

papers.title: Interactions among land use, climate, leaf litter traits, and consumers shape large-scale patterns of decomposition in streams of SW Europe
papers.authors: Diana Rojo, Javier Pérez, Naiara López‐Rojo et al.
papers.abstract: Habitat degradation is one of the primary drivers of biodiversity loss and ecosystem alteration. In streams, leaf litter decomposition plays a key role in energy and nutrient cycling, which is influenced by leaf litter quality, microbial and invertebrate consumers, and environmental conditions. Land use changes alter stream habitats and can modify decomposition rates and dynamics, but large-scale assessments of these anthropogenic impacts remain limited. We explored the consequences of major land use changes (tree plantations, agricultural land, and urban settlements) on stream ecosystems by comparing sites in human-impacted catchments with reference unimpacted sites (i.e., surrounded by native vegetation) across several regions of southwestern Europe encompassing a wide climatic gradient. We quantified decomposition rates of multiple leaf litter types to evaluate the interaction between leaf litter traits and environmental variation, exploring changes in associated invertebrate assemblages. Overall, land use changes reduced total and microbial decomposition rates, with agriculture exerting the strongest effects, and caused marked shifts in invertebrate assemblages including replacement of sensitive by tolerant species and reduced detritivore richness, mainly in urban streams. Climatic variability seemed to modulate these responses, with seasonal climates showing higher vulnerability to impacts. Lastly, leaf litter types differed in their sensitivity to detect degradation, although no consistent trait-based patterns were observed. Our results show that land use changes alter stream ecosystems across climatic gradients, highlighting the urgent need to integrate environmental and biological drivers across spatial scales in watershed management and to provide actionable baselines to optimize riparian restoration and buffer the effects of ongoing climate change.

papers.title: Operationalising connectivity in the spatial management of mangroves
papers.authors: Gabriela Thompson-Saud, Séverine Choukroun, Adam Douglas Canning et al.
papers.abstract: Mangroves form highly interconnected ecosystems, where natural rehabilitation often relies on propagule dispersal to recolonise degraded or fragmented areas where suitable hydrological and substrate conditions exist. Yet, dispersal and connectivity are rarely integrated in the spatial planning of mangroves due to limited data and a lack of operational guidance. To address this gap, we developed and tested a decision support framework that integrates mangrove connectivity and condition to guide spatial management prioritisation. Using the central Great Barrier Reef, Queensland (Australia) as a case study, we simulated dispersal of two mangrove species: Rhizophora stylosa and Bruguiera gymnorhiza, using a biophysical model driven by oceanographic currents (SLIM) and parameterised using experimentally derived propagule viability and floating duration data (IBM). Network analysis was applied to the dispersal outputs to identify mangrove sub-population importance (centrality) and key dispersal pathways that sustain connectivity processes. Habitat patches defined by five connectivity-driven management objectives were then mapped and assessed alongside satellite-derived mangrove condition (NDVI) to generate an urgency index for spatial management prioritisation. Our results identified critical areas of replenishment sources or connectivity corridors that overlapped with degraded mangrove habitats, highlighting these areas for targeted management. This framework demonstrates how explicitly incorporating connectivity into spatial planning can improve the identification of areas that may contribute to mangrove recovery and persistence under accelerating climate change and coastal development.

papers.journal: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction (IJDRR)
papers.title: Classifying perceived shaking in post-earthquake social media with large language models for rapid estimation of seismic intensity-affected areas
papers.authors: Qingle Cheng, Zhengxuan Song, Maosen Yang, Linlin Xie
papers.abstract: Rapidly characterizing the spatial extent of earthquake impacts and perceived shaking is essential for emergency response and seismic-intensity assessment. Although social media can provide abundant public feedback shortly after an earthquake, its colloquial, noisy, and sparsely geolocated content is difficult to translate into reliable impact indicators. To address the scarcity of publicly available annotated Chinese post-earthquake social media data, the limited cross-event generalization testing of existing classification models, and the insufficient integration of classification outputs with seismic-intensity estimation, this study developed a Chinese post-earthquake social media dataset containing more than 64,000 annotated Weibo comments from 12 selected earthquakes. A four-level perceived-shaking text classifier based on DeepSeek-7B and task-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) was developed and evaluated using an independent-event test and multiple leave-one-event-out tests. A population-adjusted perceived-shaking label index was further constructed to support rapid estimation of seismic intensity-affected areas. On the independent test set, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 91.34%, a weighted-average F1-score of 91.40%, and a macro-average F1-score of 89.78%, outperforming conventional machine-learning models, BERT-based models, and a zero-shot large language model. Across the multiple event tests, the macro-average F1-score ranged from 0.898 to 0.980. Compared with unclassified social media indicators, the classified perceived-shaking label indices provided better estimates of intensity-zone areas. Perceived-shaking information accumulated primarily within the first 30 min after an earthquake. The task-fine-tuned model effectively converts noisy public feedback into interpretable indicators, providing complementary support for rapid preliminary estimation of seismic intensity-affected areas.

papers.journal: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction (IJDRR)
papers.title: Bottom-up estimates of population exposure and damage from floods: A case study on Malawi's 2015 floods
papers.authors: Simon Peter Ngorok, Thomas K. J. McDermott, Jeremy S. Pal
papers.abstract: Despite the growing impacts of floods worldwide, data on their economic damages remain limited. For the universe of flood events that occur worldwide, only a subset enter standard databases such as the Emergency Events Database, and only a fraction have damage estimates. Filling this gap matters for local flood risk assessment, adaptation planning, and better accounting of climate change effects, particularly in developing countries. This paper adapts and extends the Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment Framework and Toolbox (CLIMAAX) workflow to estimate localised population exposure and direct damage from flood events. The workflow integrates the three components of flood risk: hazard, with water depths reconstructed from a satellite-derived flood extent using terrain data; exposure, from building footprints and gridded population layers; and vulnerability, through depth-damage functions. Applied to Malawi’s 2015 floods, the workflow yields rapid, localised estimates of structural damage and exposed populations in a data-scarce setting. A Radarsat-2 flood extent generated from a humanitarian emergency activation underpins the preferred estimate. The analysis indicates approximately 124,000 people exposed and direct structural damage to buildings and their contents of US$312 million (2015 US$). At matched sectoral scope, structure-only estimates of US$117–166 million bracket the US$136 million housing-sector damage reported in Malawi’s Post-Disaster Needs Assessment. Sensitivity analysis, including calibration against unit costs derived from the assessment, shows that valuation assumptions shift aggregate damages while leaving the spatial pattern of losses broadly unchanged. These bottom-up estimates complement ground-truthed post-disaster assessments and media reporting and help paint a richer picture of flood impacts.

papers.title: Modelling and addressing climate overshoots with societal stakeholders
papers.authors: Kareem Buyana
papers.abstract: Abstract Working with societal stakeholders is vital in addressing the adaptation limits and impacts of climate overshoots (exceeding the 1.5°C global warming limit). To achieve this, the paper argues that research on climate overshoots needs to be grounded in diverse methodologies that open possibilities for non-scientists to bring on board knowledge that is valuable in terms of depth (in each societal context) and comparability (across societal contexts). A reflexive approach to addressing climate overshoot impacts is proposed with the aim of shining light on how stakeholder contributions can be incorporated in projections and response actions (Singletary and Sterle, 2020; Dobre and Faldi, 2025).

papers.title: HydroSPI-ARX for explainable multi-scale drought early warning over Türkiye from ERA5 and ERA5-Land reanalyses
papers.authors: Ertuğrul Gül
papers.abstract: Abstract Machine-learning drought studies typically regress a smooth, autocorrelated index at single stations and report near-perfect fits. Temporal leakage is rarely controlled, and the skill the index already carries in its own history is rarely separated out. Here we present HydroSPI-ARX, an autoregressive and explainable framework for drought early warning over Türkiye. It recasts the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) as a leakage-controlled, lead-resolved classification target built from ERA5 and ERA5-Land hydroclimatic fields. Five drought targets are evaluated at leads of one, three, six and twelve months, with feature selection and scaling recomputed inside every training fold. The moderate-or-worse warning reaches a macro-F1 of 0.853 one month ahead, 0.794 at three months and 0.709 at six months. At twelve months it falls to 0.486, where no configuration retains skill. Naive persistence is ahead at one month; against it the framework gains 0.038 macro-F1 at three months and 0.066 at six, with year-block bootstrap intervals that exclude zero. Against a per-cell linear autoregression on the index's own memory, the gain is measurable only at six months (0.043, 95% interval 0.010 to 0.078). Exogenous hydroclimatic fields add 0.007 at one month and nothing beyond. Skill is therefore carried by the multi-scale memory of the index, and the learned model earns its place at the six-month horizon. Scoring the same held-out forecasts against station-derived labels lowers agreement (Cohen's kappa of 0.30, 0.26 and 0.21 at one, three and six months). The ranking of the forecasts survives, so the advantage is not an artefact of verifying against the same reanalysis. ERA5 and ERA5-Land are equivalent within a margin of 0.02 macro-F1 set in advance, and a model trained without a climate zone still forecasts inside it. A Mann-Kendall analysis shows rising three-month drought frequency over 1981 to 2025.

papers.title: Delayed seasonal march of East Asian summer monsoonal rain belt during Heinrich Stadials
papers.authors: Jinzhe Zhang, Ting Wei, Chuncheng Guo, Qing You Yan
papers.abstract: Abstract The timing and duration of monsoon rainfall shape regional hydroclimate, yet their response to abrupt climate change remains poorly constrained. Here, we use 25-km-resolution climate simulations to investigate the seasonal migration of the East Asian summer monsoon rain belt during Heinrich Stadials, periods associated with collapsed Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC). We find that the rain belt migrated northward 18 days later than during interstadials. This delay kept the monsoon front longer over central China, prolonging early-summer rainfall despite an overall weaker monsoon. The delayed migration was linked to later northward advances of the western North Pacific subtropical high and upper-level westerly jet. North Atlantic cooling contributed to these circulation changes through Rossby wave propagation and a weakened land–sea thermal contrast. Our results suggest that abrupt Atlantic changes can reshape both the amount and seasonal timing of East Asian summer rainfall. These findings offer a palaeoclimate perspective on potential changes in monsoon seasonality under future AMOC weakening.

papers.title: A scoping review of psychosocial factors of climate change inaction: Implications for climate change communication and education
papers.authors: Nicole M. Ardoin, Alison W. Bowers, Kathleen O’Connor, Marcia McKenzie
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate change communication and education efforts often focus on the cognitive aspects of addressing climate change, emphasizing that a key path to solving climate change-related challenges may be achieved through an educated public that better understands the science of this issue. However, despite decades of information-heavy communication and education efforts, designed with knowledge-related outcomes in mind, meaningful and sustained action to address climate change has yet to occur at a broad scale. This lack of effective, sustained action has motivated researchers from a range of fields to examine other factors that prevent climate change action. We undertook a systematic scoping review of peer-reviewed, empirical studies (n = 92) focusing on psychological and sociological (psychosocial) factors associated with climate change inaction. Through thematic analysis, we identified trends and patterns across the studies, but also noted that no obvious list of discrete psychosocial factors leading to climate inaction emerged. Political ideology and emotions were the most common factors discussed as influencing climate change inaction. Other psychosocial factors receiving notable attention included climate change perceptions, trust in institutions and leaders, values, and efficacy beliefs. The most-recommended strategies for improving effectiveness of climate change communication and education were attending to climate-related emotions; addressing issues of ideology and trust; and targeting systemic and structural barriers. Findings also emphasize that quality climate communication and education must acknowledge and build on people's unique relationships with their places, communities, and stories.

papers.title: Structuring decision-making for systemic climate-financial risk.
papers.authors: Tanya Fiedler, Monica Trezise, A. J. Pitman, Ben Rhodri Newell
papers.abstract: Abstract Physical climate risks are a source of vulnerability in financial systems, yet existing risk measurement approaches struggle to translate them into decision-relevant metrics, reflecting a mismatch between how climate risk evolves and how financial risk is assessed. Drawing on workshops and interviews with 35 finance and risk professionals (33 from a large financial institution, two from a global insurance broker), we identify six interacting risk domains through which physical climate risk cascades to credit loss, creating decision bottlenecks where routine practice breaks down. Integrating storylines and dynamic adaptive policy pathways, we develop a qualitative–analytical framework that allows decisions to proceed within these bottlenecks. Whereas scenario analysis and stress testing estimate losses under specified futures, the storylines developed here trace how risk reaches the portfolio through the responses of insurers, households and regulators and the institution itself. The pathways identify which signals to monitor and when to reconsider action, organising risk appetite as sequences of contingent actions. Because its effects lack historical precedent and a robust link to default, emerge gradually and often unseen across interacting domains, and rebound on the institution through the responses its own actions provoke, climate-financial risk is as much a problem of decision structuring and adaptive governance as of measurement.
papers.titleKo: Structuring decision-making for systemic climate-financial risk.

papers.title: Significant albedo-induced cooling effects across tropical and subtropical dryland biomes
papers.authors: Hongze Pei, Jieming Chou, Chaoyang Wang et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Terrestrial ecosystems can significantly regulate climate through carbon uptake and alterations in surface albedo. However, current climate mitigation assessments largely focus on carbon sinks while overlooking albedo-induced radiative effects. We developed an integrated framework to quantify the net climate effect of global terrestrial ecosystems from 2001 to 2019 by combining net ecosystem productivity with albedo-induced radiative forcing. We estimated the Net Equivalent Carbon Dioxide Stock Change (NESC), which incorporates both Net Cumulative Carbon uptake Equivalent (NCCE) and the Emission Equivalent of Shortwave Forcing (EESF). Results show that global terrestrial ecosystems generated a net cooling effect of 397.52 Gt CO2e during the study period. Among biomes, tropical and subtropical grasslands, savannas and shrublands, and deserts and xeric shrublands, contributed a cooling effect of 95.33 Gt CO2e due to increased albedo, nearly one-quarter of the total NCCE across the 14 biomes, largely driven by declines in photosynthetic vegetation and soil drying in Land use and land cover (LULC) non-conversion areas. These findings provide new perspectives for re-evaluating the climate value of terrestrial ecosystems and a scientific basis for incorporating surface albedo into future nature-based solutions for climate mitigation.

papers.title: GEDI spaceborne lidar for protected areas monitoring
papers.authors: Cotrina-Sanchez, A., Moudry, V., Laurin, G., Coomes, D. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Protected areas (PAs) are the cornerstone of global terrestrial biodiversity conservation, yet systematic, scalable assessment of their vegetation structural condition remains limited. NASA’s Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI), a spaceborne full-waveform lidar mission, offers a unique opportunity to consistently quantify vegetation structure within PA boundaries at near-global scales. This review synthesises 45 peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and May 2026 that use GEDI to study PAs within 26 countries on five continents. Estimates of canopy height, canopy cover, and vertical structure from GEDI’s L2A and L2B products were most widely used. Aboveground biomass density was also frequently derived, often through L4A or multi-sensor modelling. Studies of vegetation structure, carbon storage, methodological integration and multi-sensor fusion dominate the evidence base, while analyses of disturbance, biodiversity proxies, and PA effectiveness remain more limited, with only 16 studies addressing these topics. Most studies combine GEDI with optical imagery, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), airborne lidar and spaceborne lidar, field plots, or terrestrial laser scanning to support spatial mapping and validation. GEDI-derived structural metrics can support monitoring under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the Paris Agreement, and biodiversity assessments led by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), including reporting aligned with the Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBV) framework. However, this review shows that their operational use still requires stronger biodiversity linkages, clearer validation protocols, and better testing across ecosystems. Future research could further strengthen PA monitoring by integrating GEDI with new SAR and forthcoming lidar missions, and analyses using geospatial foundation models.

papers.title: Increase of tropical cyclone-induced coastal flooding due to historical sea level rise
papers.authors: Mengel, M., Sauer, I., Otto, C., Treu, S. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Surges from tropical cyclones (TCs) cause significant damage in coastal areas. However, the contribution of historical sea level rise (SLR) to surge heights and thus the flooded areas has not been quantified on a global scale. Here, we use an open-source shallow water equation solver to estimate the impact of historical SLR on coastal flooding induced by all historical TCs with landfall from 1950 to 2025, according to the International Best Tracks Archive. We isolate the SLR effect through the comparison of factual simulations accounting for observed changes in sea level to counterfactual simulations without long term trends in sea levels. Results show that SLR has steadily increased the coastal area affected by TC-induced surges, from about 5% in 1950–1954 assuming mean tide levels (7% and 5% for minimum and maximum tide levels, respectively) to about 18% in 2021–2025 (22% and 13% for minimum and maximum tide levels, respectively) in comparison to the areas affected without SLR. The increase differs along coastlines, with maxima in relative increases of surge flooding along the North American Atlantic coastline and the Southeast Asian coastline. To put the numbers into perspective, we also estimate the associated increases assuming 1 m of local SLR and no changes in TC tracks and wind fields, reaching 146% under mean tide assumptions (192% for minimum tide levels and 92% for maximum tide levels). Results show that this is higher than expected assuming a linear relationship between SLR and relative increases in flood extents. Our analysis demonstrates the significant increase in flood extent induced by SLR already today. The generated data sets of factual and counterfactual coastal flooding extend ISIMIP3a climate-related forcing data, allowing for the evaluation and attribution of additional coastal impacts.
papers.titleKo: Increase of tropical cyclone-induced coastal flooding due to historical sea level rise

papers.title: Evaluating inter- and intra-regional air pollution inequalities in a decarbonized world
papers.authors: Sampedro, J., Rodés-Bachs, C., Van de Ven, D., Tonne, C. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Ambient PM 2.5 exposure remains a major global health challenge. While pollution has declined in developed economies, it has increased in developing regions, exacerbating cross-country inequalities. Within-country disparities have narrowed in some contexts but remain significant. This study assesses how these inequalities evolve under alternative decarbonization futures, co-designed with stakeholders and aligned with current climate policy. Using an integrated assessment and air quality modelling framework, we find that international inequality in mortality burden widens over time even as income inequality across countries narrows, and that a country’s emission contribution is only moderately associated with its own exposure burden, driven more by aggregate scale than per-capita intensity. Within countries, wealthier deciles disproportionately drive emissions, but the contribution-exposure relationship shows no consistent direction, and exposure inequality itself varies enormously by country independent of income. These findings call for climate policies explicitly integrated with air quality, health, and equity objectives, tailored to where responsibility and impact diverge across scales.

papers.title: Initial affect shapes risk-benefit information processing and public support for carbon dioxide removal technologies
papers.authors: van Veen, J., Rahmani Azad, Z., Wong Parodi, G., Hahnel, U.
papers.abstract: Abstract Given the accelerating climate crisis, carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies are becoming increasingly important, while public support may play a relevant role in their implementation. This support is influenced by how citizens inform themselves about the technology. While prior research has examined public support under conditions of no or predefined information provision, little is known about the factors that shape how individuals actively select information about CDR and integrate it into their preferences about the technology. Here, we investigate how initial affect towards CDR shapes laypersons’ selection and evaluation of benefit-related versus risk-related information about the technology and how these processes influence subsequent policy support. In a preregistered study with 714 U.S. participants, we introduced a novel information-sampling task, in which participants could freely choose which information about CDR to attend to, followed by a policy choice experiment assessing public support of CDR technologies. In line with our hypotheses, participants’ initial affect influenced their information search: more initial positive affect towards CDR was associated with a higher likelihood to select benefit-related versus risk-related information about CDR. This confirmatory information search, in turn, was associated with immediate changes in affect towards the technology, especially when the information was perceived as persuasive. These affective changes across information search carried over to subsequent decisions to support climate policies in general and policy portfolios including CDR in particular. Overall, our findings highlight the reciprocal relationship between affect, endogenous information search, and support for CDR technologies.

papers.title: Incivility in public health policy discussions spills over to public engagement with climate issues: evidence from English-language social media
papers.authors: Narimanzadeh, H., Badie-Modiri, A., Smirnova, I., Chen, T.
papers.abstract: Abstract Affective polarization and political sorting drive public antagonism around climate change and other issues at the science-policy nexus. We study cross-domain spillover of incivility in public engagements with climate change and public health on English-language Twitter and Reddit using the COVID-19 period as a case study. To assess whether spillover exists between these two policy domains, we examined how the incivility of climate discussions on social media varied by their co-occurrence with COVID-19 content and temporal coincidence with pandemic events. We find strong evidence of the signatures of affective polarization surrounding COVID-19 spilling into the climate change domain. Across different social media systems, COVID-19 content is associated with incivility in climate discussions. These patterns of increased antagonism were responsive to pandemic events that made the link between science and public policy more salient. We also looked at how climate discussions about international organizations and elites changed with the pandemic’s onset to show that the observed incivility spillover activated along overlapping pre-pandemic political cleavages, specifically anti-internationalist populist beliefs that linked climate policy opposition to vaccine hesitancy. Our findings show how affective polarization in public engagement with science becomes entrenched across policy domains, which has implications for how the public engages with and communicates about issues such as climate change and public health.

papers.title: Projecting potential population exposure to the invasive malaria vector Anopheles stephensi
papers.authors: Sun, Y., Liu, W., Jing, Y., Liu, T. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Malaria remains a major global public health threat, and the recent invasion and rapid spread of Anopheles stephensi across Africa pose new challenges for disease control. To assess future risks, we estimated the distribution of An. stephensi habitat suitability under four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs, SSP126, SSP245, SSP370 and SSP585) across 2021–2100 using a boosted regression tree model, and quantified population exposure through a contribution decomposition framework separating environmental, population and joint effects. The results showed that the proportion of urban land was the most important predictor (17.17%), followed by mean temperature of the wettest quarter (BIO8, 9.24%) and the annual mean temperature (BIO1, 8.24%). Suitable habitats expanded consistently under all scenarios. Notably, SSP370 generated the highest population exposure, and there would be approximately 205.51 million people living in high suitability habitats for An. stephensi by 2081–2100. From the contribution decomposition framework, population change dominated the total exposure increase, outweighing environmental effects and joint effects. However, the individual contributions of population and environmental effects gradually declined over time, while their joint effect increased. These findings demonstrated that population growth, rather than climate change alone, is the primary driver of future exposure to An. stephensi . The increasing joint effect of population and environmental factors further underscores the need for integrated, region‐specific interventions that address their combined influence on transmission risk.

papers.title: Legionella Risk Management in Building Water Systems: Current Perspectives from Industry Practitioners
papers.authors: Hao Xi, Kirstin Ross, Greg Falzon et al.
papers.abstract: Building water systems are internationally recognised reservoirs for opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens, including Legionella, the causative agent of Legionnaires’ disease. Inadequate design, operation and maintenance can promote Legionella proliferation and expose building occupants to potentially fatal infection. Effective management is therefore critical; however, there is limited international evidence regarding how guidelines for controlling Legionella risk are implemented in practice. Despite extensive Australian guidance, little is known about the practical management of Legionella risk in building water systems. This study explored current practices among hydraulic engineers, facility managers, plumbers, and water retreatment consultants. An online survey with follow-up interviews was conducted and the responses were then compared with existing guidelines and historical case studies published in the literature. Key findings indicated that current practice is predominantly risk-focused, with monitoring, system disinfection, routine maintenance, and targeted engineering modifications forming the core control measures. Case studies demonstrated substantial variability in how practitioners select and apply interventions, reflecting the complexity and diversity of building water systems. Insufficient maintenance and poor system design emerged as the leading contributors to Legionella proliferation, while control measures failed primarily due to incorrect or inappropriate selection. Budget constraints and lack of knowledge were identified as the major barriers to implementing effective and sustained control strategies. These findings are of international relevance, highlighting the need for control measures underpinned by risk assessment and comprehensive system monitoring and providing an evidence base to strengthen guidelines for effective Legionella management in building water systems globally.

papers.title: Narrating ontologies of ruination in the disciplinary blur: Ruins as temporal gardens, trees as legal witnesses and birds as world-makers
papers.authors: Mariya Hamada
papers.abstract: This commentary investigates the disciplinary blur that challenges the dual ontology of ruination as being both an urban/architectural transformation and an ecological phenomenon. It defies categorizations of objective knowledge and comes to terms with multispecies and interdisciplinary approaches, both historiographically and ethnographically, readjusting to the multiple temporalities of the nonhuman world-making projects that the human-made ruin becomes part of. Drawing on the urban ruin of 19 th -century Manchester (Cottonopolis), England, and the architectural ruins of contemporary Mogador, Morocco, it argues that the temporalities of the nonhuman, intersected respectively with periodicities of industrial contamination and human abandonment, transform the singular obsolete narrative of ruins into a plural transdisciplinary debate questioning the unyielding becoming of urban space. The text’s historiographical and ethnographical micronarratives, woven together through storytelling, theorize the transformative temporalities of urban nature and their capacity to provide the anthropogenic ruin with a collaborative ecological agency. This, the commentary argues, adds botanical and ornithological ontologies to urban and architectural taxonomies of ruination. By positioning oneself in the disciplinary blur, the commentary ideates on how architectural and urban studies can accommodate unfamiliar rhythms of nonhuman-constructed botanical and ornithological ruins.

papers.authors: Yichao Du
papers.abstract: Why do investment-oriented municipal delegations begin with culture? This article develops cultural buffering to explain how municipal actors use cultural forms and assets when development-oriented diplomacy brings together organisations with different authority, timetables and commitments. The analysis draws on multi-sited ethnography of 5 Wuxi delegation circuits across Japan, the United Kingdom and continental Europe, followed by tracing of 21 initiatives to July 2026. It identifies two recurrent problems: municipal schedules can outrun partner learning and due diligence, while demands for visible outputs can exceed commitment and post-event ownership. Municipal actors respond to these temporal and accountability mismatches through naming, sequencing, coalition broadening and managed ambiguity. These moves can change who participates, what becomes discussable, which organisations enter the relationship and how provisional alignment is recorded. Subsequent project implementation depends on authority, resources, delivery capacity and an organisation willing to own the next step. Cultural buffering therefore identifies the encounter-level work through which an unsettled proposal becomes discussable and revisitable before its implementation is determined.

papers.title: Bridging critical knowledge and action gaps in urban health: A call for transdisciplinary approaches in urban studies in the era of global population aging and climate change
papers.authors: Vitor Pessoa Colombo, Elis Borde, Mirko Severin Winkler et al.
papers.abstract: Urbanization and population aging are two “mega-trends” posing significant challenges to global health, particularly under climate change. Despite extensive evidence on the links between the built environment and health, urban planning scholars and practitioners still miss valuable opportunities to contribute to public health and urban health equity—which often remain marginal or only implicit topics in urban planning discourses and practices. Against this background, we organized the transdisciplinary workshop “Global Health Challenges Related to Demographic & Climate Changes: Implications for Urban and Territorial Planning” (Basel, 2024), convening scholars and practitioners to co-develop a research agenda addressing knowledge-to-action gaps in urban health equity and climate resilience. Building on the workshop’s discussions, this commentary highlights current challenges in reconnecting urban planning and public health while presenting opportunities to bridge this gap. We argue for an “ultra-local” approach that acknowledges the chronic lack of granular data necessary to address spatial justice and urban health inequities, emphasizing the importance of evidence- and place-based planning. To illustrate this approach, we present two recent experiences: the BH-Viva project in Brazil, which assessed impact of slum-upgrading projects on urban health equity, and the Saint-Louis Master Plan in Senegal, a pioneering effort integrating climate resilience into urban policy and planning. Ultimately, we present what we identified as priority research paths in urban studies, having transdisciplinarity as a precondition for urban planners to effectively tackle pressing global health challenges.

papers.title: Interpreting mobility reform through care: Ambivalent authority in Taiwan
papers.authors: Francis Chia-Hui Lin
papers.abstract: This article examines how human-centred mobility reform can reproduce, rather than displace, entrenched hierarchies of automobility. Focusing on Taiwan, it analyses a regulatory archive of national traffic legislation and Taipei municipal instruments through which recent safety reforms have been articulated in the language of care, participation, and protection for vulnerable road users. The article argues that these reforms do not simply replace vehicle-centred urban order with pedestrian-oriented governance. Instead, they overlay existing mobility hierarchies with increasingly dense classifications, conditional provisions, and delegated discretion. Drawing on Homi Bhabha’s concept of ambivalence, the paper conceptualises this condition as ambivalent authority: a mode of postcolonial governance in which authority must appear protective and non-coercive while preserving inherited infrastructures of motorised priority. Through analysis of human-oriented road design, pedestrian-priority legislation, scooter and non-motorised classifications, and municipal mechanisms for temporary road use, the paper shows how care becomes a territorial technology of rule. Its contribution is threefold: it links postcolonial theory to urban mobility governance, clarifies how automobility persists through reform rather than only through resistance to reform, and reframes regulatory complexity as a political mechanism through which contradictory urban priorities are managed. The article concludes that mobility reform in Taiwan governs not by resolving the tension between care and hierarchy, but by continually recalibrating it.

papers.title: Understanding activity spaces: Contemporary issues and challenges and future research directions
papers.authors: Renee Zahnow, Jonathan Corcoran, Rebecca L. Wickes
papers.abstract: Activity spaces are a subset of locations where people spend their everyday lives. Interest in activity spaces spans the social sciences, geography, health sciences and transportation research. In recent years, the spread of smartphones and other tracking devices has made it far easier to record daily movements. This has sparked an increase in activity space research and an opportunity to consider how the concept has been conceptually and empirically defined over time and across disciplinary fields. In this scoping review, we analyse 372 studies of activity spaces published between 1972 and 2024. Despite conceptual consistency, we find that studies tend to focus, empirically, on one of four dimensions of activity spaces: access, nodes, paths and exposure. Drawing on our review, we suggest greater methodological harmonisation may better support replication and comparative studies and incremental research discovery. We propose that to achieve this, a more nuanced theoretical framework is required that defines each of the dimensions of activity space, how they are related to each other and incorporates aspects of daily activity in the new millennia (e.g. online, hybrid and multilayered time–space locations).

papers.title: Build for whom? Contested state entrepreneurialism and the governance of affordable rental housing in Shanghai, China
papers.authors: Qianyu Lu, Yang Song
papers.abstract: This paper critically interrogates state entrepreneurialism through an empirical analysis of China’s recent Affordable Rental Housing (ARH) programme. Prevailing accounts of social housing under neoliberalism tend to frame it as a residual, market-enabling instrument of welfare retrenchment. Such perspectives, however, inadequately capture contexts in which expanded provision is intertwined with intensified and reconfigured forms of state intervention. Drawing on 92 qualitative interviews in Shanghai, this paper shows how ARH operates as a strategically selective mechanism embedded within broader projects of labour governance and territorial development. While it functions as a spatial fix to absorb oversupplied housing stock amid the crisis tendencies of land-centred accumulation, its implementation reveals a fragmented and contested process of state entrepreneurialism. Intra-state frictions, bureaucratic negotiations and divergent local growth rationalities reproduce uneven and contingent outcomes, rather than a coherent developmental logic. Access to ARH is selectively structured to privilege skilled migrants, demonstrating how state housing provision is mobilised to sort labour and align welfare responsibilities with labour value extraction and urban competitiveness. Meanwhile, hierarchical state-market arrangements reproduce regulatory asymmetries and uneven access. This paper argues that social housing in contemporary China constitutes a contested terrain of accumulation and legitimation, complicating linear narratives of neoliberal convergence and advancing a more critical understanding of state-led housing provision.

papers.title: Beyond the perimeter walls: Negotiated porosity and the governance of megaproject edges in Metro Manila
papers.authors: Justin D. Stern
papers.abstract: This article examines Bonifacio Global City (BGC), an urban megaproject in Metro Manila, from the perspective of two adjacent barangays, or local government units: Guadalupe Nuevo and South Cembo. Drawing on fieldwork conducted between 2017 and 2024, it asks how these barangays manage the demands of a megaproject planned and marketed as self-contained, and how interdependence at the enclave edge becomes a basis for contesting the terms of urban porosity. Like many central business districts, BGC does not house many of the workers its economy depends on; it relies in part on adjacent barangays that provide the lower-cost housing, everyday services and mobility connections many workers require. The closure and later negotiated reopening of the J.P. Rizal butas, a long-standing informal opening in BGC’s perimeter wall, made this interdependence politically visible. From this case, the paper develops the concept of negotiated porosity. The term describes how the dependencies that sustain an enclave can become spatially concentrated at an interruptible point on its edge, allowing local government actors to contest the status and terms of access across the boundary. The article contributes to work on enclave urbanism, porous enclaves and the governance of urban megaprojects in the Philippines and beyond.

papers.title: From Frankenstein to Gulliver urbanism: Reframing AI and scale in urban theory
papers.authors: Farshad Shariatpour
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in urban governance, infrastructure and design, yet urban theory still lacks a clear language for analysing the scale asymmetries through which these systems operate. This article develops Gulliver Urbanism as a conceptual framework for understanding how AI reshapes urban power when it processes information, acts, and coordinates across cognitive, temporal and spatial horizons that exceed ordinary human capacities and institutional rhythms. Moving beyond Frankenstein Urbanism’s emphasis on rebellion and loss of control, we argue that the central problem of contemporary AI urbanism is scale asymmetry within co-constituted human and machine assemblages. The framework comprises six dimensions: cognitive scale, temporal scale, spatial scale, governance asymmetry, autonomy and agency and human response. It synthesises scholarship on AI urbanism, urban political economy, infrastructural urbanism, posthumanism, law and scale, supported by AI governance frameworks and vignettes on Hangzhou City Brain, robotaxis and generative design. The article conceptualises the urban as a constitutive condition of AI scale asymmetry, where algorithmic systems encounter infrastructure, land, mobility, public services, municipal authority, social difference and collective life. Across these domains, the key challenge is how to govern systems whose capacities outpace human oversight while remaining embedded in corporate, legal and political arrangements. We argue that effective responses require mixed-intelligence governance and temporal dignity: arrangements that subject algorithmic operations to democratic oversight, contestation and human-paced deliberation. Gulliver Urbanism explains how AI reconstitutes urban life by reorganising infrastructures, municipal authority, spatial relations, design imaginaries, public services and everyday citizenship.

papers.title: Internationalization of progressive municipalism—Barcelona international relations strategies
papers.authors: Agnieszka Szpak
papers.abstract: This article examines how the International Relations Master Plan 2020–2023 and the International Strategy 2025–2029 translate progressive municipalism into external action. Through qualitative content analysis and comparison, it identifies three mechanisms of internationalization: norm projection, networked amplification, and multilevel resource mobilization. Both Strategies promote a rights-based agenda centered on social justice, housing, democratic participation, digital rights, and ecological transition. However, the movement-oriented municipalism of the Colau administration has evolved under Collboni into a more institutionalized and partnership-based model. This shift demonstrates both the continuity and moderation of Barcelona’s progressive orientation. The article also highlights the limits of municipal internationalization: although the Strategies support agenda-setting, policy circulation, coalition-building, and access to resources, they neither confer formal international authority on the city nor guarantee implementation. Barcelona, therefore, illustrates both the potential and the structural constraints of cities seeking to influence state-centered international governance.

papers.title: Rockfall risk management on transportation corridors: coupling risk assessment with terrestrial mobile LiDAR survey on the A22 motorway (South Tyrol, Italy)
papers.authors: Francesco Lelli, Diana Bianchi, Vincenzo Critelli et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract This study presents an integrated approach, coupling rockfall risk assessment with a vehicle-based surveying for the large-scale management of slope assets along transportation corridors. Rockfall risk was assessed qualitatively using relative rating scales. To reduce the subjectivity inherent in expert judgment, susceptibility was estimated through probabilistic methods, while vulnerability was informed by conventional runout simulations. Despite the associated uncertainties, the occurrence of a January 2024 rockfall within an area classified as high risk provides independent qualitative support for the consistency of the first-level screening results. Terrestrial Mobile LiDAR (TML) survey conducted from a car was designed to maximise effectiveness and efficiency in capturing rockfall-prone slopes and establishing a baseline for long-term monitoring. Its actual effectiveness, efficiency, potential and limitations were evaluated through a survey conducted in April 2023. Approximately 3.5 km of the A22 motorway, representing more than one-quarter of the analysed section, were found to be potentially exposed to rockfall risk, originating from 27 of the 55 identified potential detachment zones. The TML survey successfully detected over 70% of these zones, achieving a point density potentially sufficient to identify volumes greater than approximately 10 dm 3 . The scanning was constrained by morphological conditions, such as vertical slopes adjacent to the motorway, structural obstacles, such as tunnel portals, and the instrument’s maximum range of 475 m. Despite these limitations, the quality and accuracy of the acquired data indicate that the TML can effectively support the motorway operators in large-scale rockfall risk management.

papers.title: Decomposing drivers of global temperature change after net zero
papers.authors: Annika Högner, Zebedee Nicholls, Gaurav Ganti
papers.abstract: Abstract Net-zero CO2 (NZCO2) and greenhouse gas emission (GHG) targets are central to the development of mitigation scenarios. Projected global surface air temperature (GSAT) change after NZCO2 depends on several factors that broadly fall into two categories: scenario-specific factors that account for the diversity of possible mitigation pathways to net zero and beyond, and model-specific factors that describe the climate system response, captured in the zero emissions commitment (ZEC). Current established climate assessment approaches do not separate contributions from these two categories to post-net-zero GSAT change in GHG emission scenarios. To address this shortcoming, we propose a diagnostic protocol that decomposes the contributions from the model-specific ZEC and from key scenario-characteristics including non-CO2 GHG reductions, net-negative CO2 emissions, and other climate forcers. We assess the GSAT outcomes from a large collection of scenarios that achieve NZCO2 using the MAGICC model. We find a peak warming increase of 0.08°C (‘likely (>66%)’ 0.05 to 0.11°C) per decade delay in reaching NZCO2 and a -0.11°C (likely -0.13 to -0.05°C) post-NZCO2 GSAT decline by 2100. Based on our decomposition approach we find that the model-specific negative ZEC contributes about -0.03°C across the full scenario set. This is on the same order as the contribution from non-CO2 mitigation for scenarios that achieve NZGHG. The decomposition allows us to test the sensitivity of our outcomes. We apply the IPCC AR6 WGI assessed value of 0°C (likely ±0.19°C) for ZEC and find that the median likelihood of no further warming on multidecadal timescales after achieving and maintaining NZCO2 drops from just about 85% to 67%. After achieving and maintaining NZGHG, however, it remains ‘very likely (>90%)’. This underlines the need for setting preventive mitigation targets to account for potential stronger than expected Earth system feedbacks and demonstrates the utility of a decomposition approach.

papers.title: Terrestrial protected areas are not effective in mitigating human pressure on biodiversity
papers.authors: Katharina Ramm, Calum Brown, Almut Arneth, Mark Rounsevell
papers.abstract: Abstract Global biodiversity is declining rapidly and protected areas are a major conservation measure aiming to reverse this negative trend by limiting pressures on biodiversity in particular locations. There are increasing calls to protect larger areas, but also growing evidence that an increase in area alone is insufficient. At least as important is the effectiveness of existing and new protected areas. We apply a novel biodiversity pressure index that encompasses the five direct drivers of biodiversity loss identified by IPBES to analyse pressures in protected areas globally. We use a GLMM to assess which variables shape the pressure levels within protected areas. We find that there are still notable human pressures in protected areas globally. Strict protection and larger size of protected areas result in lower pressures, while high national-level corruption levels result in higher pressures. The results confirm that an increase in the number of protected areas will not necessarily conserve biodiversity effectively, unless they achieve greater control of the underlying drivers of biodiversity loss, including spatially diffuse pressures and those that currently compromise small protected areas in countries with unstable governance.

papers.title: Food redistribution: a critical review of an overlooked priority measure against food waste
papers.authors: Zhang, C., Zhu, F., Song, Y., Ji, Y. et al.
papers.abstract: Abstract Food redistribution is widely recognized as a preferred strategy for reducing food loss and waste. Yet it is still treated mainly as charitable relief, while its broader role in governance and the conditions for effective implementation remain insufficiently articulated. Drawing on a triple bottom line perspective and sustainable development goal coupling framework, this study synthesizes evidence from the literature, international practice, and field research in China to examine the contributions of food redistribution, the constraints that shape its performance, and the models through which it can be scaled. We find that existing research provides much stronger evidence on social benefits than on economic mechanisms or environmental outcomes, which remain constrained by value-cost mismatches, uncertainty in substitution assumptions, and limited activity data. Cross-dimensional evaluation and analysis of synergies also remain weak. In practice, international experience points to a transferable operational architecture based on hub-and-spoke networks and standardized procedures, but successful scaling depends on aligning policy tools with operational mechanisms to reduce systemic frictions. The Chinese cases extend this understanding by identifying two complementary implementation models, centralized and decentralized, each adapted to different institutional and market conditions. Together, these findings highlight the important role of food redistribution in sustainable food and waste governance, and offer practical support for integrated evaluation and wider implementation.

papers.title: Attribution science and climate change litigation in India
papers.authors: Gill, G., Yadav, S.
papers.abstract: Abstract In climate change litigation, attribution science is increasingly being used as an evidentiary tool to ascertain responsibility, accountability, liability, and provide redress the impact on human life and the environment. The Indian judiciary implicitly uses scientific evidence in an unstructured or fragmented manner without it being clearly labelled as attribution science. This current ad-hoc reliance on scientific evidence without an identifiable scale may lead to inconsistencies in judicial outcomes, undermine legal certainty, and hinder the transparent and systematic development of climate jurisprudence. Drawing on the mathematical work of Charles Weiss, we offer an interdisciplinary explanatory climate framework that addresses the uncertainty of science by assembling a scale of legal standards arranged in a hierarchy of levels of increasing certainty familiar to the judiciary and lawyers. The originality of this article lies in extending Charles Weiss ‘standard-of-proof’ scale to address how attribution science integrates within a calibrated language of confidence and likelihood, terms used in the IPCC’s framework (Sixth Assessment Report). Reported Indian cases from the Supreme Court, High Courts and the National Green Tribunal are selected to illustrate levels of scientific certainty or uncertainty and corresponding legal standards of proof constituting acceptable bases for legal decisions in climate change litigation. The adoption of a ‘scientifically legal’ climate lexicon helps increase the precision and rationality regarding the different threshold levels for establishing causation. This article encourages next step thinking within the climate attribution adjudicative process thereby developing context-specific benchmarks that reflect India’s constitutional safeguards, precautionary ethos, and public-interest litigation traditions.

papers.title: Morphology-based classification and error-controlled reduction of urban weather files with Torino as a case study
papers.authors: Ali JahaniRahaei, Giacomo Chiesa
papers.abstract: Urban morphology creates intra-urban thermal variability that a single airport EnergyPlus Weather (EPW) file cannot represent. This study develops a reproducible GIS-to-Urban Weather Generator (UWG) framework for Torino, Italy, separating morphological classification from weather-product reduction. A preliminary building-seeded cell method was audited before adopting 100 m assignment cells characterised through overlapping 500 × 500 m neighbourhood supports. Support-size (250–1000 m) and 50 m grid-shift sensitivities were tested. Building fraction, area-weighted height, facade-to-site ratio, tree cover, and grass cover were extracted for 12,997 locations; 10,593 quality-screened supports were classified using robust scaling and CLARA-style k-medoids. Seven morphology classes balanced interpretability and spatial coherence, although four ranked best statistically, and classification robustness was moderate. Under a common UWG template, four representative EPWs were retained by curve inspection and minimax selection, with a 0.10°C maximum-error screen and a diminishing-return criterion. Maximum medoid hourly dry-bulb RMSE was 0.06°C with the delivered one-decimal EPWs and 0.04°C at diagnostic three-decimal serialisation. Across 105 stratified non-medoid supports, weighted mean and 95th-percentile RMSE were 0.05 and 0.10°C, but a 1.33°C industrial-tail error required a conservative post hoc restriction, not a validated applicability boundary. Synchronised processed 2022 station comparisons improved annual RMSE relative to Caselle only at Consolata. Humidity limitations preclude interpreting temperature fidelity as complete EPW validation. The atlas links coordinates to morphology classes, UWG configurations, and candidate EPWs. The restricted library distinguishes simulator-conditional reduction fidelity from observational accuracy.

papers.title: Environmental designs shape navigational strategies in young and older adults: evidence from an ecologically valid, virtual reality experiment
papers.authors: Maayan Merhav, Dafna Fisher-Gewirtzman
papers.abstract: Age-related declines in navigation can limit mobility and independence. Although wayfinding guidelines often emphasize landmarks, older adults increasingly rely on route-based strategies. To address this gap, we tested whether pathway configuration could support route learning and consequently improve wayfinding. Using immersive virtual reality, 76 younger (20–34 years) and 52 older (58–80 years) adults explored an environment with either a grid-shaped or star-shaped pathway layout. In the star layout, each destination was reached via a specific route, potentially strengthening route-target associations. Older adults generally travelled longer paths and showed greater distance errors. However, both age groups demonstrated better navigational memory in the star layout, reflected in smaller distance errors. This advantage was not explained by longer paths during initial exploration. Our findings suggest that pathway configuration can support route-based navigation across adulthood and highlight the potential of architectural design to improve wayfinding in public spaces.
